reviews.title: Toy Story 5
reviews.synopsis: Woody, Buzz, Jessie and the toys confront the challenges of children growing closer to technology.
reviews.verdictRationale: Provisional: friendship, loyalty and concern for children are constructive themes. The story offers discussion around belonging and technology, but is not explicitly religious.
reviews.ageRationale: Mild language, toilet humor, brief peril and an upsetting episode involving exclusion; 7+ is a cautious site recommendation.

themes.name: Love and self-sacrifice

themes.name: Family and responsibility
themes.evidence: The toys are attentive to the needs of a child.

themes.name: Compassion and service
themes.evidence: The narrative centers on caring for a lonely child.

themes.name: Profanity and blasphemy
themes.evidence: BBFC records occasional mild comic bad language.

themes.name: Violence and cruelty
themes.evidence: BBFC describes mild slapstick and non-injurious shoving.

reviews.reflection: Friendship is healthiest when it strengthens love, presence, and responsibility instead of retreating into distraction. Discuss how a Christian family can use technology without allowing it to rule relationships.

What might we miss when devices replace time together?

reviews.title: The King of Kings

reviews.verdictRationale: Provisional: the film directs attention toward Christ and the Gospel narrative. Parents should also distinguish artistic retelling from Scripture and Orthodox liturgical tradition.
reviews.ageRationale: Scenes of the Passion, a crowd threatening stoning, storm danger and Satan tempting Christ can be distressing; 10+ is a conservative suggestion.

reviews.title: Moana 2
reviews.synopsis: Moana leads a crew across dangerous seas to reconnect distant island communities.
reviews.verdictRationale: Provisional Coptic Orthodox assessment: The story strongly values leadership, family bonds, and teamwork. Its spiritually supernatural setting draws on Polynesian mythological beings and ancestral guidance, which families should distinguish from Christian prayer and providence. The overall emphasis is adventure rather than Christian formation.
reviews.ageRationale: Intense sea storms, threatening creatures, and fantasy spirituality may unsettle young viewers.

reviews.ageRationale: Extended action violence, guns, explosions, implied deaths, and a brief suicide-related incident warrant a careful age recommendation.

reviews.reflection: Power becomes morally valuable when it serves love. The family’s greatest strength is not exceptional ability but solidarity and responsibility for one another.

reviews.ageRationale: Sustained danger, manipulative emotional abuse, stabbing, and a character’s death call for age caution.

reviews.reflection: Love does not require someone to remain imprisoned by another person’s selfishness. Families can discuss the difference between protective guidance and manipulative control.

reviews.verdictRationale: Provisional Coptic Orthodox interpretation: The film affirms gratitude, ordinary joy, human relationships, and the dignity of daily life. reviews.ageRationale: Questions about death, existence, and the body–soul relationship can confuse or upset younger viewers.

themes.evidence: The protagonist reconsiders an overly narrow view of success.

reviews.reflection: Everyday life can become an occasion of thanksgiving, but the Church teaches that the human person is created by God, not assembled through the movie’s imagined pre-life program. Discuss gratitude without absorbing the invented theology.

reviews.title: GOAT
reviews.verdictRationale: The film asks viewers to admire discipline and a player’s willingness to make room for others. Will’s effort earns respect, but the story also requires star player Jett to share the ball and trust the team. It shows the limits of playing for personal glory by connecting the team’s growth to that change. The competition gets noisy and rough, yet the game’s excitement serves a story about becoming a better teammate.
reviews.ageRationale: The main concerns for younger children are hard collisions in the fictional sport, mild language and occasional comments about attraction. Start around seven if your child is comfortable with loud, fast-moving competition.
reviews.synopsis: Will Harris, a small goat who dreams of playing professional roarball, joins the Vineland Thorns and has to earn the trust of his teammates.
reviews.reflection: Teams can give a child a first experience of making room for someone else’s gifts. Ask who received encouragement before anyone knew whether they would succeed, then look for a way to give that kind of encouragement this week.

reviews.title: The Sheep Detectives
reviews.verdictRationale: The sheep’s investigation grows out of love for George, and it forces the flock to face an injustice of its own. Lily’s friendship with a ram the flock once rejected shows what their prejudice cost. A pastor’s regret about his treatment of a family adds another example of the gap between a rule and the care someone needed. The murder and the flock’s imaginative beliefs about death call for discussion, while the story gives the most weight to loyalty, taking responsibility and changing how you treat someone.
reviews.ageRationale: The story centers on a death. A body, a little dried blood, threats and scenes of grief can hit harder than the talking-animal premise suggests. Ten and up is a better starting point for children who can discuss murder as a mystery and talk through the sadness.
reviews.synopsis: When their shepherd George is found dead, Lily and the rest of the flock use what they learned from his mystery stories to investigate.
reviews.reflection: Listen to how the characters talk about the dead before offering a family answer. In an Orthodox home, this can lead to a conversation about praying for those who have died and expressing grief together.

themes.name: Loyalty through grief
themes.evidence: The flock’s love for George leads them to leave the meadow and face what happened.

themes.name: Mercy and correcting prejudice
themes.evidence: Lily befriends a formerly rejected winter lamb and confronts the flock’s custom.

themes.name: Murder mystery and peril
themes.evidence: The investigation includes a dead body, threats, ominous scenes and brief blood detail.

themes.name: Fictional beliefs about death
themes.evidence: The flock imagines that dead sheep become clouds. The story also depicts a church and a pastor who regrets an earlier decision.

questions: Why does Lily want to remember things the flock would rather forget?
What made the sheep’s rule about winter lambs seem normal to them?
How does the pastor respond when he recognizes the harm he caused?
What does the flock gain by listening to a sheep it once rejected?
How does our family remember and pray for people who have died?

themeScripture.connection: The flock learns that bearing a burden can mean staying close to another sheep when remembering hurts.

reviews.title: Superman
reviews.verdictRationale: The film holds up compassion as the reason Clark uses his power. Lex uses influence and technology to discredit and control him, and the story exposes the harm done by that appetite for control. Some clashes are played for spectacle. The central contrast, though, is between using power to protect a life and treating lives as expendable.
reviews.ageRationale: The adolescent starting point reflects repeated superpowered combat, bloody injury detail, gun threats and profanity. Families with children sensitive to characters in captivity or civilians in danger may prefer to wait.
reviews.synopsis: Clark Kent faces public distrust and a campaign against him led by Lex Luthor after intervening in an international conflict.
reviews.reflection: Compare the impulse to rescue someone vulnerable with the desire to be seen as heroic. Christian service can be costly even in situations too ordinary to draw an audience.

themes.name: Compassion and protection
themes.evidence: Clark’s concern for lives at risk motivates his actions even when public opinion turns.

themes.name: Power used for control
themes.evidence: Lex’s pursuit of control drives his schemes and threatens people around him.

themes.name: Combat and injury
themes.evidence: Extended fights, weapons, gun threats and occasional bloody injuries make the action intense.

themes.name: Profanity and insults
themes.evidence: Moderate profanity and religious exclamations recur.

questions: What changes when Clark thinks first about the person in danger?
What is Lex willing to do to protect his reputation?
Who helps Clark remember who he is when people turn against him?
Which fight scenes carry a cost the story takes seriously?
Where could we protect somebody in an ordinary situation this week?

themeScripture.connection: Read Christ’s account of serving the least and discuss why an endangered life matters independently of the reputation of the person who helps.

patristic.author: St. John Chrysostom
patristic.text: In commenting on the Last Judgment, Chrysostom points to ordinary acts such as giving water or visiting the sick. Christ takes seriously the help a person can actually give.

reviews.title: Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl
reviews.verdictRationale: The film makes Wallace’s cleverness enjoyable and shows its limits when he ignores Gromit’s concern. Feathers turns invention into an instrument of revenge, and the story makes that use of technology the threat that has to be stopped. The pair’s ingenuity works best when it grows out of loyalty and attention to each other. Comic jeopardy gives the lesson a playful setting.
reviews.ageRationale: The gnomes’ change in behavior, the chases and falls, and a brief umbrella attack may unsettle younger children. The Stage 3 guide also carries the BBFC flashing-imagery advisory.
reviews.synopsis: Wallace builds a robotic garden gnome. An old enemy, Feathers McGraw, takes advantage of the invention to settle a score with Wallace and Gromit.
reviews.reflection: In family life, convenience can save time that we then spend listening or helping. It can also become an excuse to pay less attention. Look at which of those things Wallace does with his inventions.

themes.name: Loyalty and listening
themes.evidence: Gromit stays alert to danger and uses his ingenuity alongside Wallace’s.

themes.name: Overreliance on convenience
themes.evidence: Wallace’s confidence in a clever tool makes it easier for Feathers to use it against them.

themes.name: Revenge
themes.evidence: Feathers’s return is driven by settling an old score.

themes.name: Comic menace
themes.evidence: Chases, falls and a brief umbrella attack punctuate the comedy.

questions: When could Wallace have listened to Gromit sooner?
Which jobs is Norbot good at, and what can a robot never do for a friend?
Why does Feathers keep coming back to the past?
When does Gromit show loyalty by disagreeing?
Which device in our house could free up time for one another?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s counsel about overcoming evil with good opens a conversation about the difference between stopping Feathers and taking revenge on him.

reviews.title: Mufasa: The Lion King
reviews.verdictRationale: Taka’s early welcome matters because he offers it before Mufasa has anything to give him. Later, his envy grows as the others look to Mufasa for leadership. The film shows what that envy costs their relationship and asks viewers to admire the strength Mufasa puts at the service of others. The fighting is intense enough to affect age guidance, while the contrast between service and entitlement gives the story real moral substance.
reviews.ageRationale: Lion attacks, stampedes, falls and drowning carry more emotional force than the title’s family branding might suggest. Separation from parents and bereavement may be especially difficult for younger children.
reviews.synopsis: Rafiki tells how a young Mufasa was separated from his parents, taken in by Taka’s pride and forced to travel with Taka toward a place called Milele.
reviews.reflection: Talk about the difference between wanting a role and becoming a person who can serve in that role. Then ask how a family can respond to envy while it is still small.

themes.name: Hospitality and belonging
themes.evidence: Taka helps the displaced cub find a place in the pride, setting the brothers’ relationship in motion.

themes.name: Leadership as service
themes.evidence: Mufasa earns trust through courage and care even though he has no claim by birth.

themes.name: Envy and entitlement
themes.evidence: Taka grows resentful as the group turns to Mufasa rather than deferring to Taka’s rank.

themes.name: Animal combat and peril
themes.evidence: Attacks, falls and drowning bring sustained danger to the journey.

questions: What does Taka freely give Mufasa at the beginning?
When does Taka start to think leadership is owed to him?
How can you tell that Mufasa is starting to earn other animals’ trust?
What can we do when someone close to us gets something we wanted?
Why does being able to help others matter more than having a title?

themeScripture.connection: James links bitter envy and selfish ambition with disorder. Compare that pattern with what happens to the brothers as their roles change.

reviews.title: Akeelah and the Bee
reviews.verdictRationale: Akeelah’s best choices come when she stops treating her gift as something she must either hide or prove on her own. Her neighbors help her prepare, and the rivalry becomes more generous as she recognizes what Dylan is carrying. School bullying and pressure to perform cause real harm. The film gives greater weight to learning well, accepting help and respecting an opponent.
reviews.ageRationale: School bullying includes physical contact, and guides report occasional profanity, a reference to a fatal shooting and smoking or drinking. Around ten is a reasonable starting point for discussing how grief and family expectations affect the children.
reviews.synopsis: A gifted Los Angeles middle schooler prepares for a national spelling bee with help from a demanding coach, her family and neighbors.
reviews.reflection: Christian stewardship begins with receiving a gift in gratitude and putting it to work for someone else. Ask what the championship would mean if Akeelah won it while staying indifferent to the people who helped her.

themes.name: Stewardship of talent
themes.evidence: Akeelah puts sustained work into a gift she was once reluctant to show.

themes.name: Community support and generosity
themes.evidence: Mentors and neighbors contribute to her preparation, and she comes to see Dylan as more than a rival.

themes.name: Bullying and achievement pressure
themes.evidence: School intimidation and an adult’s pressure on Dylan show the costs of fear and misplaced expectations.

themes.name: Profanity and put-downs
themes.evidence: Occasional coarse language and insults are reported in school and family settings.

questions: Why is Akeelah reluctant to let classmates see what she can do?
What does her community do that a single coach cannot?
What does Akeelah notice about Dylan once she stops seeing him as only a rival?
Which adults offer encouragement, and which add pressure?
Who could we help practice a gift they are just starting to develop?

themeScripture.connection: Peter describes using what we have received to serve one another. Notice how both Akeelah and the people who train her live out parts of that idea.

reviews.title: Wonder
reviews.verdictRationale: The story shows what cruelty costs in a child’s daily life. Jack’s hurtful remarks and later efforts to make things right give more substance to the call for kindness than a speech alone could. The film also gives Via room to feel overlooked, so compassion extends beyond the person whose struggle is most visible. It invites viewers to notice the child left out and to take the first step toward repair.
reviews.ageRationale: Bullying includes hurtful remarks about suicide and school fights. A teenager also finishes a glass of wine after an adult has been drinking heavily. Around ten is a starting point. Consider previewing the bullying scenes for a child with a similar experience.
reviews.synopsis: Auggie Pullman enters school after years of homeschooling. The story follows how that change affects him, his sister Via and classmates who have to decide how they will treat him.
reviews.reflection: An apology begins to repair something, but standing beside someone in public can cost more. Ask which characters are prepared to bear that cost after they recognize the harm they helped cause.

themes.name: Mercy and inclusion
themes.evidence: Auggie’s experience makes it clear how much ordinary acts of friendship and exclusion matter.

themes.name: Apology and restoring trust
themes.evidence: Jack and Via each face choices about how to repair strained relationships.

themes.name: Bullying and humiliation
themes.evidence: Cruel remarks and social exclusion recur, with consequences for Auggie and his friendships.

themes.name: Alcohol used during distress
themes.evidence: An adult drinks heavily under stress and a teenager finishes a glass.

questions: What does Auggie hear that changes how he sees Jack?
What makes an apology believable in this story?
How does seeing the story from Via’s perspective change our judgment?
When does helping a classmate require you to risk losing approval?
Who tends to go unnoticed in a group we belong to?

themeScripture.connection: God sees the heart when people look at outward appearance. Use the verse to think about both Auggie’s classmates and the people they overlook.

reviews.title: Hidden Figures
reviews.verdictRationale: The three women show courage by insisting that their work and preparation count. The film portrays segregated facilities and blocked opportunities as injustices with consequences for the whole team. It also lets us see how ordinary people participate in unfair systems without asking who is being excluded. The film asks viewers to admire capable, patient work and the courage to make room for other people to advance.
reviews.ageRationale: Younger viewers may need help understanding segregation, workplace humiliation and the tension of the launch. The guides also document some mild language and adult drinking. Around ten gives many children enough historical context to follow a family conversation.
reviews.synopsis: Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan and Mary Jackson put their skills to work at NASA while facing barriers based on race and sex during the space race.
reviews.reflection: Consider the difference between saying you personally have nothing against someone and examining the rules that keep them out. Dorothy’s conversation with her supervisor gives a family a concrete example of what it takes to see that distinction.

themes.name: Courage against injustice
themes.evidence: The women challenge barriers to working, learning and being recognized for what they contribute.

themes.name: Skill and responsibility
themes.evidence: Preparation in mathematics and computing gives the women tools to serve a shared mission.

themes.name: Racial and gender discrimination
themes.evidence: Segregated facilities and institutional obstacles repeatedly shape the story.

themes.name: Drinking and occasional profanity
themes.evidence: The guides mention mild language, alcohol and one conversation in which a character is visibly affected by drink.

questions: Which ordinary workplace rule creates the most obvious barrier?
What does Dorothy do when she sees that the work is about to change?
What makes telling someone about an unfair rule difficult?
Who gives another person the chance to contribute?
Where could our family notice a rule or habit that leaves somebody out?

themeScripture.connection: James warns against showing partiality. Ask how apparently ordinary routines at work could favor one person and humiliate another.

reviews.title: Nimona
reviews.verdictRationale: The story makes it easy to sympathize with a person the kingdom treats as a threat. It invites viewers to question what fear and loyalty to an institution can excuse. Ballister has to reconsider what he believes about Nimona, whose own enjoyment of mayhem is often played for laughs. That mix of compassion, comic destruction and serious emotional distress makes this a film for discussion. The film also presents a same-sex romance, which families can discuss according to their beliefs while treating the characters and real people with dignity.
reviews.ageRationale: A 13+ starting point reflects the interrupted suicide attempt, frightening rejection, fantasy violence and brief blood detail. Younger viewers can experience those moments more intensely than the animated style suggests.
reviews.synopsis: Ballister, a knight framed for a crime, looks for the truth with the help of Nimona, a shapeshifter the kingdom has taught him to fear.
reviews.reflection: Ask how to take another person’s suffering seriously even when you disagree with something they do. In an Orthodox conversation about discernment, respect for a person’s God-given dignity remains essential.

themes.name: Mercy toward the excluded
themes.evidence: Ballister’s alliance with Nimona challenges the kingdom’s assumptions about whom it can trust.

themes.name: Prejudice and scapegoating
themes.evidence: Fear of Nimona’s difference and a false accusation set the conflict in motion.

themes.name: Fantasy mayhem
themes.evidence: Sword fights, blasts and destructive set pieces include brief blood detail. Some action is played for comedy.

themes.name: Suicide-related distress
themes.evidence: One emotionally intense attempt is interrupted.

themes.name: Coarse language
themes.evidence: The BBFC documents mild terms and an implied stronger expression.

questions: What did Ballister assume about Nimona before spending time with her?
Which destructive actions does the film ask us to take seriously, and which does it play for laughs?
What could the adults have done earlier when Nimona was isolated?
How can we talk about relationships according to our beliefs and still treat people with dignity?
How can someone in our family tell us they feel alone, and how would we respond?

themeScripture.connection: James calls out the impulse to rank people by what others see first. Consider how it changes Ballister’s judgment when he starts listening to Nimona herself.

reviews.title: Home Alone
reviews.verdictRationale: Kevin grows when he stops believing the ugly story he heard about Marley, and the church conversation points both of them toward family reconciliation. The holiday comedy also spends much of its energy making painful retaliation entertaining. The warmth of the reunion gives families something worth discussing, while the story’s delight in the traps keeps the overall verdict mixed.
reviews.ageRationale: The main age concern is the repeated use of painful, potentially imitable traps in a comic register. Occasional coarse language and images including an adult magazine also appear. Discuss safe responses to strangers and emergencies with children who enjoy the slapstick.
reviews.synopsis: Kevin is accidentally left behind when his family travels for Christmas. He meets a neighbor he had been taught to fear and tries to fend off two burglars.
reviews.reflection: Ask what would be left of the story if the family reunion and Kevin’s conversation with Marley were cut. Then talk about what those scenes ask of us that the clever traps never do.

themes.name: Reconciliation
themes.evidence: Kevin and Marley encourage each other to reconnect with family after an honest conversation.

themes.name: Prayer and worship
themes.evidence: The church scene, Nativity imagery and Kevin’s prayer form a brief but important part of the Christmas story.

themes.name: Comic harm and imitation risk
themes.evidence: Painful traps are repeated for laughs, with realistic safety concerns if a child tries to copy one.

themes.name: Rumor and prejudice
themes.evidence: A frightening rumor about Marley causes Kevin to judge him before meeting him.

questions: What did Kevin believe about Marley before they talked?
Which part of their conversation helps Kevin see his family differently?
Where does the movie make pain a joke, and why might that be different in real life?
What should a child in a real emergency do to get help?
Who might need to hear from us before the next family gathering?

themeScripture.connection: Paul connects kindness and forgiveness with God’s forgiveness of us in Christ. Compare that with how Kevin and Marley change after listening to each other.

reviews.title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
reviews.verdictRationale: The story calls for courage and loyalty when fear makes the school ready to blame Harry or demean students for their ancestry. Hermione’s research and Ron’s willingness to help are among the ordinary virtues the story asks us to admire. Wizardry is also the setting’s most appealing feature and the means by which characters both cause harm and seek rescue. A family’s discernment here depends on how a child responds to the fantasy and on what the family understands by seeking spiritual power.
reviews.ageRationale: The attacks, giant spiders, threatening diary and creature confrontations are the main age factors. Around ten is a starting point for children who handle sustained fantasy fear and can discuss why the school’s prejudices are wrong.
reviews.synopsis: A series of attacks at Hogwarts leads Harry and his friends toward a hidden chamber and a diary connected to the danger.
reviews.reflection: Talk about the choices that can be practiced in real life, such as defending someone who is insulted. If the fantasy raises questions about spiritual power, explain how your household understands prayer and what it does with those questions.

themes.name: Courage and loyalty
themes.evidence: The friends research and act even when authority figures are removed and the danger grows.

themes.name: Fictional wizardry
themes.evidence: School magic and spells define the setting and are used by both heroic and threatening characters.

themes.name: Fantasy menace and creatures
themes.evidence: A hidden creature, giant spiders and attacks make this a sustained rather than brief scare.

themes.name: Ancestry prejudice
themes.evidence: Harry’s peers encounter a slur used to demean Hermione’s ancestry.

questions: Which choice shows courage even before anyone uses a spell?
Why is an insult about Hermione’s ancestry meant to wound?
What happens when a school accepts blame without proof?
Which parts of the fictional magic did you find confusing, frightening or entertaining?
How would we help someone who was targeted because of their background?

themeScripture.connection: Paul exhorts Christians to test what they encounter and hold to what is good. Ask what a viewer can learn from the friends’ actions and which parts raise questions for your household.

reviews.title: Interstellar
reviews.verdictRationale: Cooper and Murph give the search its moral weight by staying responsible for others across years of separation. The crew’s experience with Dr. Mann tests a different response to danger. His false data helps him seek rescue at others’ expense, and the film exposes what that choice costs. The long stretches of fear and grief do not erase the story’s attention to truth, perseverance and the obligations of love.
reviews.ageRationale: Infrequent strong language, a violent confrontation, prolonged space peril and scenes of separation or loss make this better suited to teens. The complicated story structure may also make it difficult for children to follow what is happening to the family.
reviews.synopsis: With Earth becoming harder to inhabit, Cooper joins a mission to look for a new home for humanity. His decision to leave changes the course of his daughter Murph’s life.
reviews.reflection: Compare the different ways characters speak about saving humanity when a particular person is in danger. A family can ask when love requires the humility to listen to someone and when it calls for a risk on someone else’s behalf.

themes.name: Love across separation
themes.evidence: Cooper’s relationship with Murph shapes both his departure and the way the mission affects people on Earth.

themes.name: Perseverance and service
themes.evidence: Murph keeps working on a problem whose solution matters far beyond her own family.

themes.name: Deception under pressure
themes.evidence: Mann falsifies his data to secure rescue and endangers the crew when his actions are discovered.

themes.name: Sustained peril and strong language
themes.evidence: Space hazards and physical confrontations sustain the tension, with occasional strong profanity.

questions: How does Murph experience the same decision differently from Cooper?
What does the crew need from Mann that only he can give them?
Why does Mann’s fear fail to justify what he does?
What keeps Murph working after she has reason to feel abandoned?
When have we kept a promise that was costly to keep?

themeScripture.connection: Read Christ’s words about laying down one’s life for friends. Discuss which characters accept a cost for others and which expect others to bear the cost for them.

reviews.title: The Fantastic Four: First Steps
reviews.verdictRationale: Galactus treats a child as the price of sparing Earth. The family refuses the bargain and still takes responsibility for the people at risk. The film asks viewers to admire courage that protects a vulnerable person alongside the wider community. Its spectacle is intense, but the story’s decisive choices favor self-sacrifice over treating someone else as expendable.
reviews.ageRationale: The threat to an expectant mother and newborn, prolonged battles, and mild coarse language make the film a better starting point at 13.
reviews.synopsis: Four superheroes face a planet-devouring alien while Reed and Sue prepare to welcome their first child.
reviews.reflection: Discuss the difference between offering something of your own and deciding someone else should be sacrificed. Ask how this applies when a group finds it convenient to leave one person out.

themes.name: Protecting the vulnerable
themes.evidence: Refusing to exchange their child for Earth’s safety is central to the conflict.

themes.name: Family solidarity
themes.evidence: The team takes responsibility for Earth and for the newborn together.

themes.name: Coercion and expendability
themes.evidence: Galactus proposes a bargain that treats a child as a means to an end.

themes.name: Superhero fighting and family peril
themes.evidence: Energy attacks, painful combat and threats to the expectant mother raise the stakes.

questions: What makes Galactus’s bargain seem tempting to frightened people?
Why does Sue refuse to treat her child as the price of solving the problem?
How do Reed and Sue’s roles as parents shape their choices?
What is the difference between risking yourself and volunteering someone else?
Who in our circle needs us to speak up when decisions are made about them?

themeScripture.connection: Christ’s words about laying down one’s own life help clarify what the film admires in Sue’s choices.

reviews.title: The Smurfs
reviews.verdictRationale: Smurfette supports a friend who worries he has no useful place, and Papa Smurf acknowledges that some of his choices hurt others. Those moments favor encouragement and accountability. The story is mainly a busy rescue comedy, with magical powers driving much of the excitement. Its moral points are worthwhile to discuss with children after the spectacle.
reviews.ageRationale: The wizards’ threats, bursts of magic and loud comic danger can unsettle young children. The BBFC notes a bleep in the UK U-rated edition. Wording may vary by cut.
reviews.synopsis: Smurfette and No Name Smurf rally the village to rescue Papa Smurf from two wizards.
reviews.reflection: A child can feel that everyone else has a clear place. Ask what Smurfette notices about her friend before he has proved what he can do.

themes.name: Encouragement and belonging
themes.evidence: Smurfette encourages No Name while he doubts that he can contribute.

themes.name: Owning mistakes
themes.evidence: Papa takes responsibility for decisions that affected his community.

themes.name: Fantasy spells and powers
themes.evidence: Wizards and magical blasts propel the rescue and its opposing forces.

themes.name: Comic threat
themes.evidence: The rescue includes blasts, pursuit and threats of being crushed.

questions: How does No Name react when he thinks everyone else has a role?
What does Smurfette do before she knows how useful her friend will be?
Why does it matter that Papa admits a mistake?
Which parts are pretend magic, and which choices can you practice in real life?
Who could you invite into a game or project this week?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s image of the body gives a family a way to ask why a group needs the member who is easiest to dismiss.

reviews.title: Gabby’s Dollhouse: The Movie
reviews.verdictRationale: Vera’s collecting has crowded out the play she once shared with Chumsley. Gabby helps them rediscover the delight of doing something together. Taking the dollhouse causes the conflict, and the story makes restored friendship more satisfying than keeping the object. The lesson is simple, and the film largely delivers it through brightly staged fantasy, including invitations to join in its pretend magic.
reviews.ageRationale: Traffic peril, a magical storm and mild body humor set the starting point. A catnip gag portrays an intoxication-like effect. The film also depicts a brief meditation scene with incense and Buddha-style figures.
reviews.synopsis: When Vera takes Gabby’s dollhouse, Gabby and her grandmother set out to recover it and reunite the toys inside.
reviews.reflection: Notice who is having fun with somebody else and who is busy trying to own something. Talk about a toy or activity that makes it easier to spend time together.

themes.name: Shared play and creativity
themes.evidence: Gabby helps Vera and Chumsley rediscover play together.

themes.name: Care and repair
themes.evidence: The pursuit of the dollhouse centers on restoring relationships and bringing the toys together.

themes.name: Pretend magic
themes.evidence: A shrinking spell, magical effects and audience participation recur.

themes.name: Meditation imagery
themes.evidence: Vera uses incense and sound bowls in front of Buddha-style cat figures in a single scene.

themes.name: Cartoon danger and rough humor
themes.evidence: Traffic and comic impacts add brief danger, with broader body humor.

questions: What does Vera hope the dollhouse will give her?
What has Chumsley missed that another collectible cannot replace?
When does Gabby share play instead of keeping it to herself?
What tells you a spell belongs to the film’s make-believe?
What could our family play together without buying anything new?

themeScripture.connection: Christ’s warning about measuring life by possessions gives a way to discuss the difference between Vera’s collecting and the pleasure of sharing play.

reviews.title: IF
reviews.verdictRationale: Bea responds to loneliness by looking for someone she can help. The story treats forgetting and growing apart as losses that deserve care. Her own fear of losing another parent gives the imaginative adventure a human purpose. Gentle scares and sentiment make it emotionally affecting, while acts of attention and companionship give it its strongest message.
reviews.ageRationale: The death of Bea’s mother is conveyed gently, but her father’s surgery and brief scares can be heavy for young children. The grief may call for an older starting point in a family facing a similar loss.
reviews.synopsis: While her father is in the hospital, Bea discovers forgotten imaginary friends and sets out to help them find companionship.
reviews.reflection: Bea’s concern for someone else can open a conversation about grief. Give a child room to talk about the parts that made them sad as well as the characters that made them laugh.

themes.name: Companionship and attention
themes.evidence: Bea works to help forgotten imaginary friends find a place to belong.

themes.name: Courage through family grief
themes.evidence: Her father’s illness gives Bea a reason to wrestle with loss while continuing to help.

themes.name: Family illness and loss
themes.evidence: Bereavement and a parent’s planned surgery shape the emotional stakes.

themes.name: Brief scares
themes.evidence: Unexpected appearances and scenes in dark places can startle.

questions: Why do the imaginary friends need help after their children grow up?
How does Bea carry both fear and the wish to help?
Who remembers what someone else has forgotten?
How can a family make room for a sad memory and a happy one?
What could we do for someone spending time alone or in a hospital?

themeScripture.connection: Paul makes room for rejoicing and weeping together. Bea’s story gives both reactions space.

reviews.title: The Journey to Bethlehem
reviews.verdictRationale: The film asks viewers to admire Mary’s willingness to receive her calling and Joseph’s willingness to care for her amid uncertainty. Herod’s threats expose the fear behind his need to protect his rank. Music and invented exchanges give the characters struggles children can discuss. Read the Nativity accounts alongside the movie, especially before treating Antipater’s role as part of the Gospel story.
reviews.ageRationale: Herod threatens mothers and babies, armed soldiers pursue the family, and a lion provides a brief scare. A parent can help younger children follow the difference between the threats and what the film shows.
reviews.synopsis: A musical retelling follows Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem while Herod searches for the child whose birth threatens his rule.
reviews.reflection: Let the film’s songs lead back to the reading of the Nativity. Ask what the birth of Christ reveals about God’s love and why it matters even without the invented scenes.

themes.name: Faith and willing obedience
themes.evidence: Mary’s response to Gabriel and Joseph’s acceptance of his role anchor the Nativity plot.

themes.name: Care for family
themes.evidence: Mary and Joseph face fear and uncertainty as they try to protect the child.

themes.name: Power and fear
themes.evidence: Herod uses intimidation to hold on to his position.

themes.name: Pursuit and dangerous threats
themes.evidence: Armed guards, a brief fight and threats against women and children raise the intensity.

questions: How does Mary respond when events go beyond what she planned?
Why does Joseph have to listen before he can act faithfully?
What is Herod afraid of losing?
Which moments can you find in Luke or Matthew, and which belong to the movie?
How might our family welcome Christ in the way we treat somebody this week?

themeScripture.connection: Read Gabriel’s announcement and Mary’s response. Compare details from Luke with the ways the musical tells the story.

patristic.author: St. Athanasius
patristic.text: Athanasius explains that the Word was truly present in a human body. His birth and ordinary bodily acts show that his humanity was real, while his deeds reveal who he is.

reviews.title: Jesus Revolution
reviews.verdictRationale: The film values welcoming people whose appearance and past make a congregation uneasy. It depicts drug use and spiritual searching as part of a world in which some characters are struggling, and it invests its hope in conversion and the possibility of a new life. Families can affirm the move toward Christ and discuss what sustained discipleship looks like within their own church tradition.
reviews.ageRationale: Drug use involving teens, car crashes, emotional crisis and verbal suicide references are the main reasons for 13+. A younger teen may benefit from watching and discussing those scenes with an adult.
reviews.synopsis: Greg Laurie encounters a growing Christian movement when pastor Chuck Smith opens his church to young people from the counterculture.
reviews.reflection: Hospitality is a choice a church member can practice before knowing someone’s story. Ask how a parish could receive a new person warmly and continue to care for them after the welcome.

themes.name: Hospitality across social divisions
themes.evidence: Chuck opens the church to young people who are visibly different from its regular attendees.

references.label: Lionsgate disc synopsis via Kalamazoo Public Library

themes.name: Conversion and belonging
themes.evidence: Greg’s encounters with the movement make Christian faith and belonging central to his story.

themes.name: Drug misuse
themes.evidence: The film depicts and discusses drug experiences as part of the characters’ struggles.

themes.name: Crisis and danger
themes.evidence: Accidents and suicide references contribute to several emotionally intense episodes.

questions: What changes when Chuck meets the people he has heard described from a distance?
How does the film connect Greg’s choices to the community around him?
When are the characters looking for spiritual meaning in something that harms them?
What would it take to welcome somebody whose experience is different from yours?
What does the film show about conversion, and what comes afterward in parish life?

sources.label: Lionsgate disc synopsis via Kalamazoo Public Library

sourceLinks.label: Lionsgate disc synopsis via Kalamazoo Public Library

themeScripture.connection: Paul connects receiving one another with Christ receiving us. Use that connection to discuss Chuck’s decision to open his church.

reviews.title: Guillermo del Toro’s Pinocchio
reviews.verdictRationale: Geppetto begins by judging Pinocchio against the son he lost. The boy’s willingness to give something up for his father helps change what Geppetto understands by love. The film distinguishes between an authoritarian demand for obedience and the responsibilities that come with caring for someone. Its strange afterlife and repeated deaths make the treatment of mortality difficult for younger viewers. The moral weight still falls on love that accepts and protects another person.
reviews.ageRationale: A child dies in a bombing, military training threatens children, and the fantasy repeatedly returns to death. The eerie images and scenes of grief make 13+ a better starting point than the PG label alone might suggest.
reviews.synopsis: A grieving woodcarver makes a puppet that comes to life in an Italy being reshaped by fascism. Pinocchio has to decide what he owes the father who made him.
reviews.reflection: Families can ask why defying cruelty differs from refusing every limit. The rules of the puppet’s fictional afterlife also give a reason to talk about how Christians understand death, resurrection and hope.

themes.name: Self-giving love
themes.evidence: Pinocchio gives up immortality to return in time to help save his father.

themes.name: Love through imperfection
themes.evidence: Geppetto has to give up comparing Pinocchio to Carlo to receive him as a son.

themes.name: Coercion and war
themes.evidence: Authoritarian leaders use children for the purposes of war.

themes.name: Fantasy death and afterlife
themes.evidence: Pinocchio repeatedly dies, encounters a personification of Death and returns.

questions: What does Geppetto expect Pinocchio to be at first?
When does refusing an order take courage?
What does Pinocchio give up for his father?
How does the story imagine death, and how does our faith speak about it?
When might we pressure someone to become who we wish they were?

themeScripture.connection: The passage connects love with what a person is willing to do for another. Consider what Pinocchio is prepared to give up.

reviews.title: Matilda the Musical
reviews.verdictRationale: Miss Trunchbull uses fear to keep children quiet. Miss Honey earns their trust by paying attention to what they need. The film asks viewers to admire the willingness to protect a classmate and challenge an abusive adult. A few acts of payback are played for laughs and Matilda uses a fantasy power. Families can separate the courage the story affirms from the way a musical exaggerates its rebellion.
reviews.ageRationale: Shouting, intimidation, child neglect and physical threats are sustained even when staged comically. The BBFC also gives a flashing-imagery warning. Ten and up can be a better fit for discussing cruel treatment at school and home.
reviews.synopsis: Matilda finds allies in a kind teacher and librarian as she stands up to neglect at home and cruelty at school.
reviews.reflection: Ask where a child could safely turn for help at home, school or church. Miss Honey gives us a good example of an adult a child can approach.

themes.name: Courage and advocacy
themes.evidence: Matilda speaks and acts when classmates are endangered or humiliated.

themes.name: Care for children
themes.evidence: Miss Honey and the librarian give Matilda support the other adults withhold.

themes.name: Cruelty and abuse of authority
themes.evidence: Trunchbull’s intimidation and assaults drive the school conflict.

themes.name: Fantasy telekinesis and payback
themes.evidence: Matilda uses a fictional power and sometimes responds to cruelty with pranks.

questions: What makes Miss Honey someone Matilda can trust?
Which school rules are used to protect children, and which are used to frighten them?
When does a prank change the situation, and when does it hurt somebody?
Which adult could you tell if someone were hurting a classmate?
What can a person do when rules are being enforced unfairly?

themeScripture.connection: The call to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves fits Matilda’s willingness to defend other children.

reviews.title: The Sea Beast
reviews.verdictRationale: Maisie respects the people who raised and protected her and still asks whether they are wrong about their enemies. The adventure gives bravery a second meaning when Jacob has to reconsider what he has been taught. Early combat is exciting and some creatures are injured. The story asks viewers to pay attention to the harm done by an inherited war and to admire someone who dares to tell the truth about it.
reviews.ageRationale: Cannons, spears, enormous creatures and dark fluid from an injury create sustained peril. Mild profanity and tavern drinking also appear. Younger children who fear giant animals may need to wait.
reviews.synopsis: Maisie stows away on a hunting ship and challenges Jacob’s assumptions about the giant sea creatures he has been raised to fight.
reviews.reflection: Ask what someone owes a teacher or hero when that person is wrong. It can be possible to acknowledge what we received from them and still decline to repeat a harmful decision.

themes.name: Truth-seeking courage
themes.evidence: Maisie questions the stories that taught her whom to fear and asks Jacob to look at what happens himself.

themes.name: Peacemaking and compassion
themes.evidence: An encounter with the creatures gives the characters a reason to reconsider the fighting.

themes.name: Violence against animals
themes.evidence: Cannons, muskets and blades are used during sustained battles with giant creatures.

themes.name: Entrenched mistrust
themes.evidence: Accepted stories and inherited loyalties help to keep the conflict going.

questions: What did Maisie expect of a famous hunter before she met one?
What does she learn by seeing a creature up close?
Why might Jacob find it hard to admit that people he admires could be wrong?
Which action makes peace possible?
What is one fair way to check a story that makes another group sound dangerous?

themeScripture.connection: Christ calls peacemakers blessed. Discuss which choice actually makes peace possible in the film.

reviews.title: The Truman Show
reviews.verdictRationale: The show within the film treats Truman as a product and calls its control protection. The movie gives him the clearest moral authority when he starts to seek the truth despite the cost. His decision to risk the sea exposes how far the producer is willing to go to keep an audience. That criticism of manipulation weighs more heavily than the film’s unsettling premise and ironic humor.
reviews.ageRationale: The created storm and depiction of drowning, staged intimacy, coarse language and the idea of a whole community deceiving one person make this a better conversation for teens.
reviews.synopsis: Truman begins to suspect that the town he has lived in all his life is part of a television production.
reviews.reflection: The film gives a producer power over a manufactured world. Ask how that desire for control differs from the Christian understanding of love and freedom.

themes.name: Courage to seek truth
themes.evidence: Truman keeps looking for an explanation when those closest to him tell him his doubts are mistaken.

themes.name: Human dignity and freedom
themes.evidence: The film gives moral weight to his right to choose a life outside the production.

themes.name: Deception for profit
themes.evidence: Staged relationships, surveillance and manufactured fears protect the show’s commercial interests.

themes.name: Drowning and storm peril
themes.evidence: The film uses a drowning incident and dangerous water conditions to portray fear and control.

questions: When do people call the show’s control a form of protection?
Why can someone feel safer believing a lie?
What does Truman risk in order to know the truth?
What responsibility does the audience have for the producer’s choices?
Where in ordinary life do people deserve more privacy than they are given?

themeScripture.connection: Paul links open truthfulness with renouncing deception. Consider how the television production depends on practices the passage rejects.

reviews.title: The Sound of Music
reviews.verdictRationale: Maria’s patience and music help the children reconnect with their father. The Captain’s refusal to serve the new regime gives the family’s private commitments a public cost. The convent offers help when that choice makes them vulnerable. The film asks viewers to admire a household held together by care and a conscience that can withstand pressure.
reviews.ageRationale: The last act brings soldiers, a gun threat and a tense escape. Young children may need help with the Nazi setting and the long running time.
reviews.synopsis: Maria becomes governess to the von Trapp children, and their new family faces increasing pressure as the Nazis take power in Austria.
reviews.reflection: Consider how warmth and discipline can work together in a family. Then ask what makes courage possible when doing the right thing puts someone’s comfort or safety at risk.

themes.name: Family care and reconciliation
themes.evidence: Maria helps the children and the Captain recover a shared family life.

themes.name: Conscience under pressure
themes.evidence: The Captain refuses an order to serve the Nazi regime, and the convent helps the family.

themes.name: Intimidation and persecution
themes.evidence: The regime’s demands and pursuit put the family in danger.

themes.name: Brief armed threat
themes.evidence: The escape brings soldiers and a gun threat, with little physical violence.

questions: What changes in the house after the children begin singing?
Why is it hard for the Captain to listen to Maria at first?
What might he have lost by going along with the orders he received?
What do the nuns risk in helping the family?
When can a family help someone who is afraid to stand alone?

themeScripture.connection: The apostles put obedience to God above human commands. The Captain’s refusal gives families a way to discuss conscience under pressure.

reviews.title: The Hunchback of Notre Dame
reviews.verdictRationale: Frollo makes his own desire and prejudice sound like someone else’s fault, and uses authority to threaten Esmeralda and humiliate Quasimodo. The film directs sympathy toward the people he mistreats and admires Esmeralda’s refusal to leave them undefended. The frightening songs and images demand care, but the story makes mercy and resistance to cruelty more compelling than Frollo’s power.
reviews.ageRationale: Sexual obsession, threatened execution, fire and frightening religious imagery make 13+ a reasonable starting point for discussion despite the US G rating.
reviews.synopsis: Quasimodo, a cathedral bell-ringer kept apart from the city, encounters Esmeralda and sees how the judge who controls him treats outsiders.
reviews.reflection: Ask how a person can use religious words to avoid examining their own conduct. Then look at how the film portrays charity in the choices of people who protect others.

themes.name: Mercy and defense of outsiders
themes.evidence: Esmeralda protects Quasimodo and stands up to the judge on behalf of others.

themes.name: Loyalty and courage
themes.evidence: Quasimodo risks his safety to help the friends who treat him with dignity.

themes.name: Cruelty and abuse of authority
themes.evidence: Frollo’s threats, prejudice and public humiliation drive the conflict.

themes.name: Coercive desire and intense imagery
themes.evidence: Frollo’s song and threats turn his obsession into a source of fear and danger.

questions: When does Frollo blame someone else for a choice he is making?
Why does Esmeralda defend a person the crowd mocks?
Who treats Quasimodo as someone capable of making his own choices?
How can religious language serve the truth or conceal wrongdoing?
What can we do when someone in a group becomes an easy target?

themeScripture.connection: The Pharisee and the tax collector offer a way to discuss how self-justification can hide pride and contempt.

reviews.title: Cars 3
reviews.verdictRationale: Lightning initially measures his usefulness by whether he can still win. Cruz understands what it is like to have somebody assume you do not belong on the track. The story asks us to admire the change in Lightning as he begins to offer another racer the attention and opportunity a mentor once gave him. The crash and derby provide excitement, while sharing a chance to race gives the film its clearest account of success.
reviews.ageRationale: The opening crash and demolition derby are louder and more intense than much of the film. Seven and up is a starting point for children sensitive to crashes or injury.
reviews.synopsis: A crash puts Lightning McQueen’s career in doubt. A younger trainer, Cruz Ramirez, helps him return to racing and challenges what he thinks his next chapter should be.
reviews.reflection: Ask a parent, coach or grandparent to tell a story about a mentor. Think of one thing you have learned that you can now help another person practice.

themes.name: Mentorship and generosity
themes.evidence: Lightning learns to offer Cruz a chance to take her own abilities seriously.

themes.name: Perseverance and adapting to change
themes.evidence: Lightning reconsiders what he can contribute as younger racers surpass him.

themes.name: Racing crashes and peril
themes.evidence: A major wreck and the demolition derby bring sharp bursts of danger.

themes.name: Dismissal and rivalry
themes.evidence: Rivals dismiss Lightning and the film gives weight to Cruz’s experience of being underestimated.

questions: What does Lightning think success means just after the crash?
What talent does Cruz see in herself by the end?
What did Doc Hudson give Lightning that he can give somebody else?
Why can sharing an opportunity be harder than giving advice?
Who could we encourage to try something they have been told is beyond them?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s counsel to look to the interests of others fits Lightning’s shift from defending his own place to supporting Cruz.

reviews.title: Toy Story 4
reviews.verdictRationale: Woody first sees caring for Forky as another way to carry out the job he knows. Forky’s need to belong, and Gabby Gabby’s questionable pursuit of the same thing, widen his view of what another toy may need. Gabby’s pressure for Woody’s voice box creates a genuine moral conflict. Woody’s later generosity gives the audience more reason to admire freely offered help than the attempt to take what somebody else has.
reviews.ageRationale: The antique shop’s ventriloquist dummies, chases and separation fears can alarm younger children, especially those sensitive to dolls or getting lost.
reviews.synopsis: Woody tries to keep Bonnie’s new homemade toy Forky safe during a road trip and reunites with Bo Peep along the way.
reviews.reflection: Ask why generosity has to be freely given. Gabby’s desire for someone to care about her explains her behavior and gives Woody an opening to help.

themes.name: Care for the vulnerable
themes.evidence: Woody spends much of the trip trying to keep Forky safe and help him understand that Bonnie values him.

themes.name: Generosity and change
themes.evidence: Woody chooses to help Gabby and has to rethink what his own future looks like.

themes.name: Pressure and manipulation
themes.evidence: Gabby Gabby uses her control of the antique shop to pursue Woody’s voice box.

themes.name: Scary dolls and pursuit
themes.evidence: The antique-shop dummies and pursuit create several tense family-film sequences.

questions: Why does Forky have trouble believing he matters to Bonnie?
What does Gabby try first when she wants help?
What makes a freely given gift different from taking something?
What is hard for Woody about changing roles?
Who could use help feeling that they belong right now?

themeScripture.connection: Paul describes love as patient and unwilling to insist on its own way. Compare that with Woody’s choice about how to help.

reviews.title: Ferdinand
reviews.verdictRationale: Ferdinand is repeatedly told that his size obliges him to be aggressive. The film gives moral weight to his refusal to perform cruelty for a crowd. His courage includes caring what happens to the other bulls, so it goes beyond insisting on his own preferences. Some chase and rough comedy are played for laughs, but the central test is whether he will become what other people expect.
reviews.ageRationale: Bullring danger and the threat of slaughter machinery can frighten children who are especially sensitive to animals in danger. There is also mild crude humor.
reviews.synopsis: A peaceful bull is taken from the home where he grew up and expected to fight in a bullring.
reviews.reflection: Ask what Ferdinand does with his strength when someone tries to provoke him. A family can talk about how to be gentle without leaving somebody else undefended.

themes.name: Gentleness and self-control
themes.evidence: Ferdinand resists pressure to prove his worth by fighting.

themes.name: Friendship and peacemaking
themes.evidence: He values companionship and the safety of other animals over competition.

themes.name: Cruel pressure to perform
themes.evidence: The bullfighting setting repeatedly treats the animals according to their usefulness in the ring.

themes.name: Animal peril
themes.evidence: The ring and slaughterhouse machinery introduce potentially upsetting danger.

questions: What do the other bulls assume a strong bull should be like?
When does Ferdinand need to be brave without fighting?
What makes it hard for someone to change a group’s expectations?
How does the film want us to feel about the bullring?
Where in our lives can we use strength gently?

themeScripture.connection: Paul writes about refusing to repay evil for evil. Discuss why Ferdinand’s restraint takes real courage in the ring.

reviews.title: Ron’s Gone Wrong
reviews.verdictRationale: The company offers friendships that can be counted and customized. Ron’s failures force Barney to consider what two friends actually owe each other. The movie invites us to notice how public embarrassment and social status can change the way a child sees a classmate. Comic chaos is part of the appeal, while the story favors giving time and attention freely over trying to automate belonging.
reviews.ageRationale: Public humiliation, bullying, coarse language and several frantic danger sequences are the main age concerns. Children old enough to encounter messaging or social platforms may get the most out of the discussion.
reviews.synopsis: A lonely boy receives a malfunctioning robot built to be the perfect friend, and the two have to figure out friendship for themselves.
reviews.reflection: Talk about a time a friend needed attention when it was inconvenient. Ask whether a device helped you know they needed you or got in the way of noticing.

themes.name: Friendship and loyalty
themes.evidence: Barney and Ron learn to understand each other through shared trouble.

themes.name: Care and belonging
themes.evidence: Barney’s loneliness makes the support of his family and others matter.

themes.name: Bullying and public humiliation
themes.evidence: Social exclusion and embarrassing incidents shape how the children treat each other.

themes.name: Dependence on technology
themes.evidence: The B*Bot’s promise of a ready-made friend is tested against Barney’s real experience with Ron.

questions: Why does Barney think a B*Bot will solve his problem?
Which things does Ron have to learn by spending time with Barney?
How does embarrassment change the way children treat one another?
When does a screen help a friendship and when does it make things worse?
What can you offer a friend who feels left out?

themeScripture.connection: The proverb connects friendship to loyalty in adversity. Compare this with what happens when Ron and Barney are embarrassed or in trouble.

reviews.title: The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader
reviews.verdictRationale: The dangers at sea put the travelers’ private temptations in the open. Lucy struggles with comparison, and Eustace’s greed has consequences he cannot undo by himself. The film gives greater weight to recognizing weakness and accepting help than to mastery of the ship’s dangers. Aslan’s role makes grace and moral change natural subjects for a Christian family conversation.
reviews.ageRationale: Sea battles, a menacing serpent and Eustace’s frightening transformation make ten a reasonable starting age. Younger children may need help distinguishing the film’s supernatural threats from its Christian symbolism.
reviews.synopsis: Lucy and Edmund return to Narnia with their cousin Eustace and sail with Caspian in search of missing lords.
reviews.reflection: Talk about the kind of help Eustace needs after he has done wrong. In family life, asking for help can be the beginning of repair.

themes.name: Humility and change
themes.evidence: Eustace’s choices and his need to accept help give the voyage its clearest moral transformation.

themes.name: Courage and loyalty
themes.evidence: The travelers continue together when fear and temptation threaten their mission.

themes.name: Envy and greed
themes.evidence: Lucy’s comparison and Eustace’s attraction to treasure threaten their judgment.

themes.name: Fantasy combat and supernatural peril
themes.evidence: A dragon, fighting and frightening danger at sea give the voyage moments of intense peril.

questions: When does Eustace begin to see what his choices have cost?
Why does comparison make it harder for Lucy to value what she has?
Who helps someone else face a fear?
What kinds of problems can’t the travelers solve alone?
What temptation gets easier to see when you talk about it honestly?

themeScripture.connection: James traces what happens when desire is allowed to grow into action. Ask where the travelers could have turned back before their choices took hold.

reviews.title: The Chronicles of Narnia: Prince Caspian
reviews.verdictRationale: Peter wants to take charge and ignores Lucy when she asks him to wait for Aslan. The cost of the castle raid gives the story a reason to question pride even when it comes from a hero. The attempted return of the White Witch presents a shortcut to power that the story treats as dangerous. The film values courage more when it comes with the humility to listen and the patience to trust.
reviews.ageRationale: Sword and arrow battles, deaths and an attempted summoning with a blood offering make this more intense than its PG rating may suggest. Ten and up is a starting point for children comfortable with sustained fantasy combat.
reviews.synopsis: The Pevensie children return to a changed Narnia and help Prince Caspian resist the ruler who has taken power.
reviews.reflection: Ask how confidence changes when people stop listening. A Christian family can talk about patience and discernment before acting, especially when others will bear the consequences.

themes.name: Faith and patient courage
themes.evidence: Lucy continues to trust Aslan before the others accept her account.

themes.name: Pride and grasping for control
themes.evidence: Peter dismisses Lucy’s counsel and leads the costly raid.

themes.name: Violence in war
themes.evidence: The struggle for Narnia includes sustained sword and arrow combat, with consequences for the heroes’ side.

themes.name: Temptation through forbidden power
themes.evidence: The White Witch is invoked in an ominous ritual as a supposed solution to military danger.

questions: Why is Peter reluctant to wait?
What does Lucy notice that the others dismiss?
Who pays for the decision to attack the castle?
What makes the offer of the White Witch tempting?
When have we confused confidence with wisdom?

themeScripture.connection: The proverb about pride and a fall helps explain why Peter’s courage alone is insufficient.

reviews.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
reviews.verdictRationale: Frodo sees in Gollum both a danger and a person shaped by the Ring’s power. His willingness to spare him gives compassion a place amid the fighting, and Sam’s suspicion gives families a fair question about caution. The defense of Rohan and the journey to Mordor place courage alongside endurance, mercy and loyalty. Intense warfare shapes the age recommendation.
reviews.ageRationale: Sustained siege combat, frightening creatures and injury detail make this best approached from 13. The extended cut differs from the theatrical version and may warrant checking the edition.
reviews.synopsis: Frodo and Sam travel toward Mordor with Gollum as their guide while their friends help defend Rohan.
reviews.reflection: Discuss how to help a person while staying honest about the harm they can do. Compare Frodo’s concern with Sam’s concern for safety.

themes.name: Mercy amid mistrust
themes.evidence: Frodo continues to treat Gollum as someone worth sparing while Sam questions the risk.

themes.name: Perseverance and loyalty
themes.evidence: Friends hold to their responsibilities as the journey and the defense of Rohan become more dangerous.

themes.name: Corrupting power
themes.evidence: The Ring’s hold on Gollum shows what obsession can do over time.

themes.name: Siege warfare and fantasy horror
themes.evidence: Helm’s Deep and other conflicts bring sustained combat and frightening enemy designs.

questions: Why does Frodo see more in Gollum than Sam does?
What is Sam right to worry about?
What makes courage possible when victory seems unlikely?
How do different characters respond to the chance to control others?
What would patient loyalty look like in a difficulty we face today?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s call to overcome evil with good gives a way to discuss whether Frodo can recognize evil and still choose mercy.

reviews.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King
reviews.verdictRationale: The film gives Sam’s patient service as much importance as military victory. The Ring reveals how even a person with a good purpose can become possessive, and the outcome makes earlier acts of mercy matter. The battles are large and frightening, yet the central moral achievement belongs to people who accept a cost to help others and keep going after they have lost confidence.
reviews.ageRationale: Prolonged warfare, deaths, a terrifying spider and distressing final scenes justify a teen starting point. This guidance is for the theatrical film. Check the edition if watching the extended version.
reviews.synopsis: As Gondor faces invasion, Frodo and Sam attempt the last part of the journey toward Mount Doom.
reviews.reflection: Ask why someone struggling with a burden may still need friendship even after their judgment becomes hard to trust. Think about a practical act that makes it easier for someone to keep going.

themes.name: Faithful friendship
themes.evidence: Sam stays close when the strain of the Ring changes how Frodo treats him.

themes.name: Sacrifice and leadership
themes.evidence: Characters accept real risk so others have a chance to survive and finish the mission.

themes.name: Obsession and despair
themes.evidence: The Ring’s appeal distorts judgment and pushes characters toward destructive choices.

themes.name: Epic combat and horror
themes.evidence: Large battles, frightening creatures and the giant spider sustain fear and peril.

questions: When does Sam offer help that Frodo cannot give himself?
How does the Ring change what a character thinks belongs to them?
Whose earlier mercy matters at the end?
What does the film ask us to admire about Aragorn’s leadership?
How can we support someone who is losing hope?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s invitation to bear one another’s burdens helps a family discuss what Sam can and cannot carry for Frodo.

reviews.title: Mulan
reviews.verdictRationale: Mulan’s deception makes sense in light of her desire to protect her father, and the film gives it consequences when she loses the trust of her companions. Her courage becomes more convincing when she continues to help people who have doubted or dismissed her. The ancestral spirits and Mushu are important to the movie’s fantasy. Families can discuss those depictions alongside its account of duty and courage.
reviews.ageRationale: Animated battles and threats from invading troops can be frightening. There is mild innuendo around the disguise, and the film presents active ancestral spirits. Seven and up is a reasonable starting point with discussion.
reviews.synopsis: Mulan takes her father’s place in the army and hides her identity while training to defend China.
reviews.reflection: Compare concern for a parent’s well-being with concern for what others will think of the family. Ask how truth affects the trust Mulan needs.

themes.name: Family duty and sacrifice
themes.evidence: Mulan takes a serious risk to keep her father from being sent to war.

themes.name: Courage after rejection
themes.evidence: She continues to protect people after her disguise is exposed.

themes.name: Deception under pressure
themes.evidence: Mulan’s disguise helps her protect her father and later creates a crisis of trust.

themes.name: Ancestral spirits and wartime peril
themes.evidence: Mushu and the ancestors influence the plot alongside animated conflict.

questions: Why does Mulan think she must act?
What does her disguise accomplish and what does it cost?
Who changes their mind about her?
How can we talk about the ancestral spirits respectfully from our own faith?
What is one way to honor a parent without worrying about appearances?

themeScripture.connection: Christ’s words about laying down one’s life invite discussion about the risk Mulan accepts to protect her father.

reviews.title: Monsters, Inc.
reviews.verdictRationale: The company has built its work around making children afraid. Sulley’s care for Boo forces him to see the harm hidden in an ordinary job. The discovery about laughter changes what the whole city is able to value. Chases and monster scares can unsettle children, but the film gives its moral weight to protecting a child and changing how a community treats people it once feared.
reviews.ageRationale: Bedroom monsters, the threat of a machine that frightens children and suspenseful chases may affect children already afraid at bedtime. Around seven is a starting point for children sensitive to these scares.
reviews.synopsis: Two workers at a company powered by children’s screams have to protect a young girl who wanders into their world.
reviews.reflection: Ask where Sulley’s responsibility begins. A family can talk about going along with an ordinary routine until someone shows us who is being hurt.

themes.name: Care for a child
themes.evidence: Sulley prioritizes Boo’s safety even when doing so threatens his work.

themes.name: Changing a harmful practice
themes.evidence: Laughter shows that the city can thrive without depending on terror.

themes.name: Exploitation through fear
themes.evidence: The company pursues power by frightening children and goes to dangerous lengths to keep doing it.

themes.name: Monster scares and chases
themes.evidence: An unseen pursuer and the factory equipment add suspense to the rescue.

questions: What does Sulley believe about children before meeting Boo?
When does his attitude begin to change?
Why is it hard for workers to question how their company operates?
How does laughter change what the monsters value?
Who could we make feel safer this week?

themeScripture.connection: Christ’s words about receiving a child give a way to think about Boo’s effect on Sulley.

reviews.title: The Emperor’s New Groove
reviews.verdictRationale: Kuzco is funny even when he is unkind. The film lets the audience laugh at his pride while showing what it costs Pacha and his family. Pacha offers help without giving up his responsibility to defend his home. Their relationship gives the ending its moral force because Kuzco learns that his power affects people he has never bothered to know.
reviews.ageRationale: Name-calling, animal threats and a fictional transformation potion accompany fast-moving slapstick. The danger is largely comic, with occasional brief scares.
reviews.synopsis: A selfish emperor turned into a llama needs help from a villager whose home he planned to destroy.
reviews.reflection: Ask what helping someone looks like when that person has wronged you. Pacha keeps the interests of his family in view alongside his concern for Kuzco.

themes.name: Humility and consideration
themes.evidence: Kuzco has to depend on a man whose home he was prepared to take.

themes.name: Mercy and boundaries
themes.evidence: Pacha helps Kuzco while continuing to defend his family’s needs.

themes.name: Selfish rule and betrayal
themes.evidence: The emperor’s entitlement and the villain’s schemes set the conflict in motion.

themes.name: Comic peril and transformation
themes.evidence: Fictional potions and bursts of slapstick create short dangers.

questions: When does Kuzco first listen to Pacha?
Why does Pacha help someone who has harmed him?
What does Pacha still have a right to protect?
Which jokes show us the cost of Kuzco’s pride?
Who could we listen to before making a decision that affects them?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s counsel to look to the interests of others gives a way to talk about what Kuzco learns from Pacha.

reviews.title: Pinocchio
reviews.verdictRationale: Pleasure Island promises Pinocchio freedom from responsibility and then reveals the people exploiting that desire. His lies and poor judgment carry real costs. The film asks viewers to admire honesty, a willingness to listen and the courage he shows when someone else is in danger. The boys’ transformation can be frightening even for children who follow the moral lesson.
reviews.ageRationale: The boys’ transformation, a whale attack, apparent drowning and scenes of children smoking or drinking make seven a suggested starting point. Consider the child’s comfort with disturbing transformations.
reviews.synopsis: A wooden puppet brought to life has to learn which voices to trust as he hopes to become a real boy.
reviews.reflection: Ask why someone offering fun might want a child to stop listening to people who care for them. Practice how to tell an adult when an invitation feels wrong.

themes.name: Truthfulness and conscience
themes.evidence: Pinocchio faces repeated choices between deception, shortcuts and listening to wise counsel.

themes.name: Courage for someone else
themes.evidence: Pinocchio risks himself when Geppetto needs help.

themes.name: Peer pressure and exploitation
themes.evidence: Pleasure Island uses apparent freedom to draw the boys into danger.

themes.name: Smoking and frightening transformation
themes.evidence: The boys’ smoking and drinking accompany frightening consequences at Pleasure Island.

questions: Why does Pleasure Island seem enjoyable at first?
Which adults are trying to gain something from Pinocchio?
When is telling the truth harder than avoiding trouble?
What choice shows that Pinocchio is thinking of Geppetto?
How can you check an invitation that asks you to keep it from your family?

themeScripture.connection: Read the warning about being enticed and discuss what makes the offer of Pleasure Island hard to refuse.

reviews.title: Fantasia
reviews.verdictRationale: The film asks its audience to respond to music and imagery across several largely independent segments. The apprentice learns about taking on power without responsibility. The final pairing moves from a threatening night scene to the quiet procession set to Ave Maria. These moments invite reflection, while the anthology as a whole is primarily an artistic experience with varied spiritual images.
reviews.ageRationale: Some mythological figures are unclothed in stylized animation. The nighttime segment includes a devil-like figure and ghostly imagery. Ten is a suggested starting point for children able to discuss images that might be upsetting.
reviews.synopsis: Animated segments pair classical music with stories and images ranging from ballet and mythology to a frightening night scene and a closing procession.
reviews.reflection: Consider watching individual segments together. Ask what changes when the film moves from fear to stillness.

themes.name: Attention and appreciation of music
themes.evidence: Music supplies the structure and emotional direction of the anthology.

themes.name: Responsibility after misusing power
themes.evidence: The apprentice loses control of the magic he uses to avoid work.

themes.name: Infernal fantasy imagery
themes.evidence: The night sequence uses a devil-like figure and ghostly designs.

themes.name: Stylized nudity and intoxication
themes.evidence: The mythological segment includes exposed bodies and Bacchus drinking.

questions: What do you notice when a scene has no dialogue?
What mistake does the apprentice make before the trouble begins?
Which musical change makes the night sequence feel different from the procession?
Which images felt unsettling even when you knew they were animated?
Which segment would you choose to show someone who is learning to listen closely?

themeScripture.connection: Use the passage to discuss what each segment draws your attention toward and how the music shapes that response.
