reviews.title: The NeverEnding Story
reviews.verdictRationale: Bastian starts as a reader looking for shelter. The story gives him reason to act when he recognizes that his response matters. Atreyu experiences loss rather than winning every trial by being brave. The film asks viewers to value imagination that helps a person respond to trouble, while its darkness makes that invitation especially demanding for younger children.
reviews.ageRationale: The horse sinking in the swamp, a frightening wolf, bullying and a brief glimpse of charred remains can be upsetting. Ten is a suggested starting point, particularly for children troubled by animal peril.
reviews.synopsis: Bastian retreats from bullying into a book about a young warrior trying to save a world threatened by the Nothing.
reviews.reflection: Tell children they can talk about the horse scene even if they cannot explain why it upset them. Bastian and Atreyu give a family two ways to discuss acting in the face of fear.

themes.name: Courage and participation
themes.evidence: Bastian learns that the story requires an answer from him, even though he is afraid.

themes.name: Imagination and hope
themes.evidence: Reading opens a world in which refusing despair has consequences.

themes.name: Bullying and despair
themes.evidence: Bastian’s exclusion and the threat of the Nothing show different forms of isolation.

themes.name: Animal loss and fantasy terror
themes.evidence: The swamp, menacing wolf and other frightening images can be deeply unsettling.

questions: What is Bastian trying to escape when he starts reading?
How does Atreyu respond after he loses a companion?
What is one fear Bastian has to face?
How can a story give someone courage in ordinary life?
Who could you turn to when you feel alone?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s prayer for hope offers a way to discuss how hope works when sadness is real.

reviews.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
reviews.verdictRationale: Elliott’s first response to E.T. is fear, and his encounter with the stranded visitor teaches him how to care for someone he hardly understands. The children act because they see the visitor’s vulnerability before the authorities do. The film gives loyalty and a willingness to let a friend go more weight than the thrill of pursuit.
reviews.ageRationale: The invasion of the home, armed pursuit and severe illness or apparent death can be distressing. There is mild language and an intoxication scene played partly for laughs. Ten is a suggested starting point.
reviews.synopsis: Elliott shelters a stranded alien and, with his family and friends, tries to help him contact home.
reviews.reflection: Ask what kindness costs Elliott once helping his friend means accepting their separation.

themes.name: Hospitality and compassion
themes.evidence: Elliott offers shelter to a visitor who cannot provide it for himself.

themes.name: Loyalty and letting go
themes.evidence: The children help E.T. return home even as the experience of friendship makes parting painful.

themes.name: Capture, illness and fear
themes.evidence: Armed pursuit, medical intervention and an apparently dying character create prolonged tension.

themes.name: Comic intoxication
themes.evidence: E.T. drinks beer and Elliott’s behavior mirrors the effects.

questions: What changes between Elliott’s first encounter and his decision to help?
How do the children know what their friend needs?
Which adults understand the danger differently?
Why does helping E.T. go home cost Elliott something?
What could hospitality look like in our home this week?

themeScripture.connection: The call to show hospitality to strangers gives families a question to bring to Elliott’s first choices.

reviews.title: Big Hero 6
reviews.verdictRationale: Hiro’s grief makes the wish for revenge easy to understand. It also makes him willing to use Baymax in a way that defeats the robot’s purpose of helping people. The support of his friends and the memory of Tadashi give him another way to respond. Superhero spectacle is part of the film, but the story asks what a person does with skill and power when they have every reason to be angry.
reviews.ageRationale: The death of a loved one, the fire and prolonged battles are intense even without graphic injury detail. Ten is a starting point for discussing Hiro’s grief and anger.
reviews.synopsis: A young inventor coping with his brother’s death joins friends and a healthcare robot to uncover a dangerous plot.
reviews.reflection: Ask what would make Baymax a faithful reminder of Tadashi. Think about a talent you can put to work to help someone who is hurting.

themes.name: Care and service
themes.evidence: Baymax’s role as a caregiver gives purpose to the technology and shapes Hiro’s choices.

themes.name: Friendship during grief
themes.evidence: Hiro needs the help of friends while facing the loss of his brother.

themes.name: Vengeance and misuse of power
themes.evidence: Hiro’s desire to hurt the person he blames leads him to misuse a robot built to care.

themes.name: Action violence and loss
themes.evidence: A deadly fire and continuing fights with futuristic technology sustain the peril.

questions: Why did Tadashi build Baymax?
When does Hiro’s anger start to change how he treats his friends?
How does trying to get justice differ from trying to hurt someone back?
Which choice best honors Tadashi?
How might a skill we have help someone who is grieving?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s instructions about vengeance invite a discussion about Hiro’s choice of what to do with his anger.

reviews.title: The Karate Kid
reviews.verdictRationale: Cobra Kai teaches Daniel’s rivals to prove themselves by intimidating opponents. Miyagi demands patience and discipline before Daniel understands how the work will help him. The tournament is exciting, but what gives the movie substance is its distinction between learning to defend yourself and defining strength by your ability to hurt someone. Discuss the brief unexplained healing scene on its own terms.
reviews.ageRationale: Bullying, martial-arts injuries, profanity, an unwanted kiss and a brief apparent drug reference make ten a better starting point than the tournament plot alone suggests.
reviews.synopsis: Bullied by local karate students, Daniel learns from Mr. Miyagi how to respond and prepare for a tournament.
reviews.reflection: Think of a time someone helped you become more patient by asking you to practice something ordinary. What was hard to see about that lesson at first?

themes.name: Discipline and wise mentorship
themes.evidence: Miyagi’s training makes patience and repetition part of learning to defend oneself.

themes.name: Restraint and courage
themes.evidence: Miyagi models a different use of skill from Cobra Kai’s aggression.

themes.name: Bullying and intimidation
themes.evidence: Daniel’s rivals repeatedly harass or threaten him.

themes.name: Martial-arts combat and injury
themes.evidence: The fights are a source of excitement and include bruising and some bleeding.

questions: Why does Daniel get impatient with Miyagi’s methods?
What does each teacher mean by strength?
Which scenes show the harm done by Cobra Kai’s bullying?
When is walking away harder than responding?
Who is someone whose patient instruction you can thank?

themeScripture.connection: The proverb values self-control over outward strength. Compare what each teacher rewards in his students.

reviews.title: Bolt
reviews.verdictRationale: Bolt has been taught that saving Penny depends on his special powers. On the road he has to trust companions who tell him the truth and help him live as an ordinary dog. The studio’s deception gives way to courage and loyalty that survive without the show’s tricks. The action mostly serves that lesson, though the flights and chases may frighten children.
reviews.ageRationale: The staged attacks, later chases and danger to animals are the main concerns. Around seven is a reasonable start for a child who can tell the show-within-the-film scenes from the story’s actual danger.
reviews.synopsis: A television dog who believes his powers are real gets lost and relies on a stray cat and a hamster to find Penny.
reviews.reflection: Talk about the people who tell us the truth even when it is uncomfortable. Real courage is easier to recognize after Bolt loses confidence in his powers.

themes.name: Loyalty and friendship
themes.evidence: The long trip gives Bolt and his companions repeated opportunities to help each other.

themes.name: Courage without recognition
themes.evidence: Bolt learns he can help Penny without the powers that made him famous.

themes.name: Deception for entertainment
themes.evidence: Keeping Bolt convinced that the show is real causes him preventable fear and distress.

themes.name: Chases and threats to animals
themes.evidence: Staged attacks and other action threaten Bolt and his friends.

questions: Why does Bolt trust the story the studio tells him?
What does Mittens teach him about ordinary life?
What changes when his friends see him frightened?
What gives his actions value after he realizes the powers were staged?
Who is someone who helps you see what is real?

themeScripture.connection: The proverb’s attention to the honest wounds of a friend gives a way to discuss how Mittens helps Bolt.

reviews.title: Mary Poppins
reviews.verdictRationale: The musical gives Mr. Banks more than a lesson about having fun. His concern for order and his position at work make it hard to hear what his children need. The shared time at the end shows a change in what he treats as important. The film’s magic is part of its imaginative staging, while its most useful invitation is to notice who needs your attention at home.
reviews.ageRationale: A few alleyway scares and slapstick moments may startle. The BBFC’s later classified edition notes dated discriminatory language, a brief indirect suicide reference and flashing imagery.
reviews.synopsis: A magical nanny visits the Banks household and helps two children reconnect with their busy parents.
reviews.reflection: Think of an ordinary family activity. Ask what would make it show attention to one another instead of feeling like one more task to complete.

themes.name: Parental attention and reconciliation
themes.evidence: The parents learn to make room for the children’s needs and spend time with them.

themes.name: Imagination and joy
themes.evidence: Music and playful ideas help the children and adults approach ordinary tasks differently.

themes.name: Work and status crowding out family
themes.evidence: Mr. Banks’s attachment to his role at the bank keeps him from noticing the children’s unhappiness.

themes.name: Scares and stage magic
themes.evidence: Alleyway scares and impossible adventures punctuate the story.

questions: What does Mr. Banks notice about work that he misses at home?
When does play help a character listen to somebody?
What does the final kite scene show about the family?
What responsibility can children and parents share?
What could we spend time doing together this week?

themeScripture.connection: Paul addresses how parents bring up children. Discuss what the children are asking of Mr. Banks and why it takes him so long to hear them.

patristic.author: St. John Chrysostom
patristic.text: Commenting on Paul’s words to parents, Chrysostom warns against overbearing treatment of children and asks parents to raise them with the Lord’s instruction.

reviews.title: Onward
reviews.verdictRationale: Ian wants experiences with his father that he never had. The search gradually shows him how much care and courage his brother has already offered. The film makes grief understandable and asks the viewer to admire Ian’s decision to see what Barley needs. The fantasy ritual is central and warrants its own discussion, especially in a family trying to understand Christian hope after a death.
reviews.ageRationale: The plot deals with a parent’s death and a fantasy spell intended to bring him back. A dragon, fire and other dangers add intensity. Ten is a starting point, with extra care for children affected by recent loss.
reviews.synopsis: Two elf brothers have one day to complete a spell that could let them see their late father again.
reviews.reflection: Talk about how a family remembers someone who has died and how it recognizes the people who are helping now. Explain how your Christian tradition speaks about hope and prayer for the departed.

themes.name: Brotherly loyalty and care
themes.evidence: The road trip helps Ian recognize Barley’s acts of care and accept a cost for him.

themes.name: Grief and gratitude
themes.evidence: Ian’s wish to see his father gives way to noticing the relationships already supporting him.

themes.name: Fantasy return of the dead
themes.evidence: The attempt to bring their father back for one day drives the plot.

themes.name: Fantasy danger
themes.evidence: Fire, traps and a dragon create several stretches of peril.

questions: What does Ian think he needs at the start?
When do you notice something Barley has done for Ian?
Why does the ending matter to both brothers?
How does the film’s fantasy differ from the way we talk about death and hope?
Who helps our family remember someone we miss?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s words about considering the interests of others fit Ian’s change of focus toward what his brother needs.

reviews.title: Wolfwalkers
reviews.verdictRationale: Robyn has been taught to see the wolves only as a danger. Her friendship with Mebh gives her a reason to question the Protector’s use of force. The story also gives her father a difficult responsibility as he chooses whether to listen to his daughter. The film invites compassion for the people and creatures the town fears. Its folklore and its fictional portrayal of religious authority deserve a conversation alongside the courage it affirms.
reviews.ageRationale: The confrontations include weapons, animal peril and death. Look for a child’s comfort with threats to parents, wolves and frightening transformations before choosing this as a family film.
reviews.synopsis: A hunter’s daughter befriends a girl who can become a wolf and has to reconsider why the adults want the wolves gone.
reviews.reflection: Distinguish Robyn’s growing compassion from every decision she makes while disobeying. Ask how a family can listen to evidence that changes what it believes about a neighbor.

themes.name: Empathy and friendship
themes.evidence: Robyn’s relationship with Mebh changes whose safety she takes seriously.

themes.name: Protecting family and community
themes.evidence: Robyn and her father face costs as they learn to care for others beyond their own household.

themes.name: Coercion and prejudice
themes.evidence: The Protector insists on obedience and uses force against those who oppose him.

themes.name: Folklore and armed peril
themes.evidence: Human-to-wolf transformations accompany armed confrontation and danger to the animals.

questions: What does Robyn think a hunter should do at first?
What persuades her that the wolves deserve protection?
When does her father finally listen?
What makes the Protector’s exercise of authority harmful?
When can hearing someone’s own story change how you see them?

themeScripture.connection: The proverb says the first account can sound right until it is examined. Ask what Robyn learns after she meets Mebh.

reviews.title: How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World
reviews.verdictRationale: Grimmel treats creatures as things to hunt and control. Hiccup has a different temptation because he cares for Toothless and still finds it hard to imagine giving up their old life. The movie gives its strongest moral weight to a leader who accepts the cost of letting a friend go. Fast action and danger make the adventure intense, while that choice gives it a reason for families to return to it afterward.
reviews.ageRationale: Weapons, fire, venom and threats to dragons recur. Around ten is a starting point for viewers sensitive to fights, animals in danger or a sad farewell.
reviews.synopsis: Hiccup seeks a safe home for the dragons while Grimmel pursues Toothless and threatens Berk.
reviews.reflection: Ask how someone can love a friend while allowing them room to grow. Think of a situation where helping required giving up some control.

themes.name: Love and freedom
themes.evidence: Hiccup considers Toothless’s future even when it means changing their relationship.

reviews.title: The SpongeBob Movie: Search for SquarePants
reviews.verdictRationale: SpongeBob lets somebody else define what courage should look like and lands in danger trying to prove himself. The friendship and help he receives give families a better measure of courage. The movie spends most of its energy on jokes, battles and supernatural spectacle, so the strongest reflection comes from the contrast between bravado and accepting help.
reviews.ageRationale: Ghost pirates, curses, sword fights and cannon fire can startle young viewers. Brief cartoon nudity and mild innuendo also appear.
reviews.synopsis: SpongeBob joins the ghostly Flying Dutchman on an underworld voyage to prove he is brave.
reviews.reflection: Ask what a friend can do when someone is about to take a risk just to impress another person.

themes.name: Courage and friendship
themes.evidence: The voyage tests SpongeBob’s ideas about bravery and the value of help.

themes.name: Admitting fear
themes.evidence: Courage develops alongside fear rather than as invulnerability.

themes.name: Ghosts and curses
themes.evidence: The Flying Dutchman and his crew make supernatural fantasy central to the voyage.

themes.name: Comic fighting
themes.evidence: Sword fights and cannon fire are recurring sources of excitement.

questions: What does SpongeBob want to prove?
Who gains something when he tries to look fearless?
When does accepting help take courage?
How do the ghost scenes mix scares and jokes?
How could you help a friend who feels pressured to prove something?

themeScripture.connection: Use the proverb about wise counsel to discuss whose advice SpongeBob would have benefited from hearing.

reviews.title: Despicable Me 4
reviews.verdictRationale: Gru protects his family, but the film also turns Poppy’s blackmail and a theft into sources of comedy. Maxime’s revenge is treated as a genuine wrong, while the heroes’ shortcuts receive less scrutiny. Family loyalty gives the story some warmth. Its main appeal is still the chase and the joke.
reviews.ageRationale: Cartoon fights, villain threats and a brief taser incident sit alongside toilet humor and a quick comic exposure of a Minion’s backside.
reviews.synopsis: Gru and his family take new identities after a former rival escapes, and a neighbor draws Gru into another scheme.
reviews.reflection: Compare the way the movie treats Maxime’s revenge and Poppy’s pressure. What would taking responsibility look like in either situation?

themes.name: Family loyalty
themes.evidence: Protecting the family sets Gru’s main choices in motion.

themes.name: Blackmail and theft

What does Poppy expect Gru to do for her?
Which of Gru’s choices make his family safer?

reviews.title: Kung Fu Panda 4
reviews.verdictRationale: Po wants to hold on to a role that gave him a sense of purpose. Taking Zhen seriously asks more of him than winning another fight, because he has to give someone with a difficult past room to change. The Chameleon’s pursuit of other people’s abilities shows the cost of treating gifts as things to seize. The martial arts and the story’s spiritual-world fantasy merit their own discussion.
reviews.ageRationale: Frequent martial-arts action, a threatening sorceress and returning adversaries may be intense for young children.
reviews.synopsis: Po looks for a successor and enlists the help of Zhen, a thief who knows where to find a shape-changing sorceress.
reviews.reflection: Talk about what you would look for in a person you wanted to teach. Po has to notice what a pupil could become.

themes.name: Mentoring and letting go
themes.evidence: Po has to choose and help prepare a successor.

themes.name: Growth and second chances
themes.evidence: Zhen’s past does not settle what she is able to choose next.

themes.name: Sorcery and transformation
themes.evidence: The Chameleon’s powers drive much of the conflict.

themes.name: Martial-arts combat
themes.evidence: Recurring fights dramatize danger and provide much of the action.

questions: What does Po fear about leaving his old role?
What does Zhen need to learn from Po?
What could Po learn from Zhen?
Why does the Chameleon want others’ powers?
Which skill could you pass on to somebody else?

themeScripture.connection: Paul’s account of passing on what one has learned gives a way to reflect on Po’s responsibility to a successor.

reviews.title: The Lord of the Rings: The War of the Rohirrim
reviews.verdictRationale: Wulf’s grief becomes a reason to punish people who had no part in his loss. Héra’s commitment to helping her people gives the story another account of strength. The film asks viewers to admire leadership that keeps others alive, even as the siege makes its violence a sustained part of the experience.
reviews.ageRationale: This is an animated siege drama with stabbings, strangling, blood and a severed limb. The age guidance reflects that sustained violence and the grief of wartime loss.
reviews.synopsis: Héra helps defend Rohan when Wulf pursues revenge for the death of his father.
reviews.reflection: Ask where grief becomes permission to hurt someone else and what a leader owes civilians when tempers are high.

themes.name: Leadership under siege
themes.evidence: Héra and her family help defend a threatened people.

themes.name: Courage to protect others
themes.evidence: The defense asks what leaders owe their community under extreme pressure.

themes.name: Vengeance and pride
themes.evidence: Wulf’s desire to avenge his father is the central cause of the siege.

Where does Héra show leadership apart from fighting?
How do pride and grief affect the leaders?
How would you help someone who feels they have to settle a score?

themeScripture.connection: Read Paul on vengeance and overcoming evil with good. Compare what Wulf seeks with what Héra tries to protect.

reviews.title: Harold and the Purple Crayon
reviews.verdictRationale: Harold’s crayon makes creativity entertaining, and the story briefly gives that gift a purpose when Harold and Mel talk about loss. Gary wants the same power to get his own way. The family insight is worthwhile, while the movie mostly asks viewers to enjoy what a magical crayon can make possible.
reviews.ageRationale: Brief weapon threats, bullying, the loss of a parent and a bloody nose are the main concerns. The crayon’s magical effects include a climactic fight.
reviews.synopsis: Harold brings his purple crayon into the real world and meets a boy who is grieving his father.
reviews.reflection: Ask how you can respond to a friend who tells you that something they miss cannot be replaced.

themes.name: Creativity to help

reviews.title: Wish
reviews.verdictRationale: Magnifico talks about protecting his kingdom as he keeps people’s wishes under his control. Asha’s resistance is driven by concern for her family and eventually her neighbors. The film asks viewers to admire taking responsibility for one another. The star and sorcery are central fairy-tale devices, and their role is worth addressing alongside the film’s ideas about hope.
reviews.ageRationale: Dark magic, magical attacks and a threatening ruler can scare young viewers. Seven is a starting point for children who handle sustained fairy-tale peril.
reviews.synopsis: Asha seeks help from a wishing star after discovering that the king controls which dreams can be pursued.
reviews.reflection: Talk about a hope that can be pursued by helping one another. Consider what a real person owes the people who entrust something important to them.

themes.name: Courage for the community
themes.evidence: Asha acts on what she learns about the wishes entrusted to the king.

themes.name: Solidarity
themes.evidence: The people of Rosas are asked to take part in changing what happens to them.

themes.name: Control over others
themes.evidence: Magnifico’s treatment of the wishes drives the conflict.

themes.name: Sorcery and magical threat
themes.evidence: The wish, the star and the king’s darker magic shape the fantasy conflict.

questions: Why do people hand over their wishes?
What does Asha see that changes her mind about the king?
When does a promise to protect become controlling?
What distinguishes the wishes in the movie from prayer?
What is one hope we can act on by helping somebody else?

themeScripture.connection: Ask what doing justice and walking humbly would require from someone with Magnifico’s authority.

reviews.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem
reviews.verdictRationale: The brothers want acceptance, and April helps them see how their choices affect the people they want to know. Superfly responds to rejection by deciding that others deserve to suffer. The movie challenges that revenge, though ridicule and frantic combat often provide the laughs. Families have something to discuss about belonging and about the ways the film uses embarrassment for comedy.
reviews.ageRationale: Rapid foot and weapon fights, a giant monster battle, comic electrocution and crude jokes make ten a suggested starting age.
reviews.synopsis: The turtle brothers ask April for help connecting with humans and face a mutant who wants to turn rejection into revenge.
reviews.reflection: Ask how being rejected can influence the way a group treats people outside it.

themes.name: Belonging and loyalty
themes.evidence: The brothers work together while trying to build trust with humans.

themes.name: Refusal to retaliate against a group
themes.evidence: The turtles and April take a path different from Superfly’s revenge.

themes.name: Crude ridicule
themes.evidence: Embarrassment and bodily-function jokes become comic material.

themes.name: Cartoon combat
themes.evidence: Weapons, martial arts and a giant creature battle make the action sustained.

How does April help them understand what others see?
What does Superfly do with the pain of rejection?
Which jokes make somebody else’s embarrassment the point?
How can we respond when another group treats us unfairly?

themeScripture.connection: Paul asks Christians to consider how they respond when someone does them wrong. Compare the turtles’ choices with Superfly’s.

reviews.title: Trolls Band Together
reviews.verdictRationale: The brothers’ old urge to perform perfectly together helped pull them apart. Saving Floyd requires paying attention to a brother they have lost touch with. The villains show the opposite by using someone’s gift for their own popularity. The music keeps the story light, yet the reconciliation gives it something a family can carry home.
reviews.ageRationale: The capture and draining of a singer, brief threats and mild innuendo may affect younger children. Seven is a starting point for children comfortable with comic captivity.
reviews.synopsis: Branch reunites with his brothers after singers kidnap Floyd to exploit his musical abilities.
reviews.reflection: Talk about a family occasion when getting the performance right crowded out listening to somebody.

reviews.title: Chicken Run: Dawn of the Nugget
reviews.verdictRationale: Ginger has good reason to fear the factory, and Molly’s danger shows what can happen when comfort is used to disguise exploitation. Ginger must act on both her daughter’s need and the needs of the other chickens. The story draws humor from the machinery and the break-in, while giving its real weight to protecting the vulnerable.
reviews.ageRationale: There is sustained danger from factory machinery, sharp tools and a food-processing line. Parent-child separation and the threat to the chickens may be upsetting.
reviews.synopsis: After Molly leaves the island where her family lives, Ginger leads an effort to rescue her from a chicken-processing factory.
reviews.reflection: Ask why attractive surroundings can make danger harder to recognize. Look for people the film treats as worth helping even after the central rescue seems possible.

themes.name: Care for family
themes.evidence: Ginger’s effort to reach Molly drives the rescue.

themes.name: Solidarity with captives
themes.evidence: The chickens take responsibility for others exposed to the same mistreatment.

themes.evidence: The factory hides its purpose behind attractions designed for the chickens.

themes.name: Machinery and captivity
themes.evidence: The production line and armed threats put the rescue in sustained jeopardy.

reviews.title: Leo
reviews.verdictRationale: Leo begins by thinking about what he wants to do with the time he has left. The students’ worries give him a different reason to spend that time. The film treats practical kindness and listening as things that help children grow, even though crude jokes and a threatening substitute sometimes pull attention away from that insight.
reviews.ageRationale: School anxieties, crude and suggestive jokes, and an alligator chase appear. Ten and up is a starting point for children who can discuss both the advice and the jokes.
reviews.synopsis: An aging classroom lizard starts listening to fifth graders after they discover he can talk.
reviews.reflection: Ask what a child gains from being heard before an adult starts giving advice. Think of one worry you could make room to hear.

themes.name: Listening and empathy
themes.evidence: Leo starts responding to the worries the students share with him.

themes.name: Self-giving and mentorship
themes.evidence: The classroom pet finds a new purpose in helping other people.

themes.evidence: The comedy includes suggestive jokes and a brief cartoon rear view.

themes.name: Childhood social pressure
themes.evidence: School conflicts give the children fears to talk about.

themeScripture.connection: James’s call to be quick to hear fits the change in Leo’s attention to the children.

reviews.title: Peter Pan & Wendy
reviews.verdictRationale: The film gives the feud a history and shows that injury can keep people tied to the past. Wendy sees reasons to value home and growing up even though Neverland is exciting. The story treats reconciliation and taking responsibility as more mature responses than continuing the rivalry. Pirate threats are sustained enough to need separate age guidance.
reviews.ageRationale: Children face pursuit, sword fights and execution threats. Ten is a starting point for those sensitive to children being in danger or separated from family.
reviews.synopsis: Wendy follows Peter to Neverland and confronts a feud between Peter and Captain Hook while considering what it means to grow up.
reviews.reflection: Talk about the difference between keeping a sense of play and refusing the responsibilities that come with growing older.

themes.evidence: Peter and Hook’s past gives the story room to ask whether they can repair harm.

themes.name: Growing in responsibility
themes.evidence: Wendy’s decisions ask what growing up can make possible.

themes.evidence: Hook’s grievance and Peter’s refusal to face the past prolong the feud.

reviews.title: Lightyear
reviews.verdictRationale: Buzz treats correcting his mistake as his responsibility alone. Working with younger teammates gives him a reason to reconsider that approach. The loss of time and of a friend makes this more than a space chase, though the action and fictional time travel carry much of the film. The parent guide also records the affectionate portrayal of Alisha and her wife for families who want to discuss it.
reviews.ageRationale: Robots, explosions, laser fighting and the death of an older friend may upset sensitive children. The parent guide includes the brief kiss between Alisha and her wife.
reviews.synopsis: Buzz’s attempts to get his stranded crew home move him into a future where a younger team needs his help.
reviews.reflection: Discuss how taking responsibility differs from insisting that only you can repair a mistake.

themes.name: Teamwork and trust
themes.evidence: Buzz learns to work with people whose abilities he initially doubts.

themes.name: Humility after mistakes
themes.evidence: The mission tests Buzz’s faith in his ability to solve everything alone.

themes.name: Danger and science-fiction combat
themes.evidence: Lasers, explosives and attacking robots recur.

themes.name: Loss and longing for the past
themes.evidence: Time dilation separates Buzz from people whose lives are moving on.

reviews.title: Minions: The Rise of Gru
reviews.verdictRationale: Gru learns to value the Minions’ loyalty, and his relationship with Wild Knuckles gives him a reason to reconsider whom he can trust. The film also makes the goal of becoming a villain part of its appeal. The jokes often make theft and outlaw status seem exciting, so the loyalty gives families something to affirm within a mixed story.

reviews.synopsis: A young Gru hopes to join a group of villains and gets into trouble after taking an object they want back.
reviews.reflection: Ask which traits make someone a good mentor and whether loyalty requires going along with everything a friend does.

themes.name: Loyalty and teamwork
themes.evidence: The Minions keep helping Gru through the consequences of his choices.

themes.name: Comic admiration of villainy
themes.evidence: The plot gets laughs from Gru’s ambition to become a supervillain.

themes.evidence: Gru takes the object that draws the villains after him.

themes.name: Cartoon combat and monsters
themes.evidence: Fights, a threat over fire and magical transformations sustain the action.

reviews.title: DC League of Super-Pets
reviews.verdictRationale: Krypto fears that Lois will take his place in Superman’s life. reviews.title: Strange World
reviews.verdictRationale: Searcher wants his son to value the life he chose, just as his own father expected him to become an explorer. The adventure gives both men reasons to listen and to reconsider what they owe their home. The film’s main moral weight lies in repairing family trust and taking responsibility for the place they depend on. Ethan’s crush on a boy is part of his story and can be discussed with dignity and according to the family’s beliefs.
reviews.ageRationale: Large creatures, pursuit and the possibility of losing a parent can unsettle younger children. The film also includes affectionate scenes and Ethan’s crush.
reviews.synopsis: Three generations of the Clade family explore the unfamiliar world beneath their home and reconsider what they want for one another.
reviews.reflection: Ask a child to name one skill or interest that feels like their own. Consider how a parent can show interest without deciding what it must become.

themes.name: Repairing family trust
themes.evidence: The Clades have to listen across several generations to work together.

themes.name: Responsibility for a shared home
themes.evidence: The expedition forces the family to reconsider what keeps their community alive.

themes.evidence: Expectations passed from father to son repeatedly strain the relationship.

themes.evidence: Large fantastical animals threaten and pursue the family.

themeScripture.connection: Use Paul’s guidance to parents to discuss how to encourage a child without pressuring them to repeat a parent’s choices.

reviews.title: Sonic the Hedgehog 2
reviews.verdictRationale: Sonic wants to be a hero before he understands who may get hurt by rushing in. Knuckles gives the story a chance to consider what loyalty looks like when someone has misled you. Those lessons come through clearly, although the film’s main attractions are fights, speed and the pursuit of a power-granting object. Families can talk about what being responsible contributes to a rescue.
reviews.ageRationale: Explosions, tasers, robots and sustained comic fighting may be intense for younger viewers.
reviews.synopsis: Sonic and Tails try to reach a powerful emerald before Robotnik and Knuckles can use it.
reviews.reflection: Compare Sonic’s early desire to look heroic with the way he eventually learns to rely on others.

themes.name: Responsibility and compassion
themes.evidence: Sonic grows in his understanding of whom his choices affect.

themes.name: Trust and teamwork
themes.evidence: The fight over the emerald gives Sonic and his companions reasons to cooperate.

reviews.title: The Chosen: Season Three Finale
reviews.verdictRationale: The finale gives disciples room to struggle with trust and with pain that is difficult to share. The feeding scene asks the viewer to attend to Christ’s compassion, while the marital conflict invites reflection on how people respond to suffering at home. The production gives the biblical story imagined dialogue and character histories. Reading the Gospel account alongside the episodes helps families identify where the screenwriters have added to it.
reviews.ageRationale: References to suicide and the death of a child, marital strain and a discreet injury image justify a teen starting point. The Australian classification lists no violence in its table and describes the injury in its written advice.
reviews.synopsis: The theatrical presentation of Season Three episodes seven and eight brings Simon and Eden’s strained relationship alongside the gathering Jesus feeds.
reviews.reflection: Let the episodes prompt a conversation about trust in Christ when prayer and family life feel difficult. Give family members room to share what they recognize in the disciples’ struggles.

themes.name: Compassion and provision
themes.evidence: Jesus’ care for a large gathering anchors the feeding scene.

themes.name: Trust amid uncertainty
themes.evidence: The stories of the disciples and the gathering repeatedly return to questions of faith.

themes.name: Marital strain
themes.evidence: Simon and Eden’s crisis forms an important secondary thread.

themes.name: Grief and distressing references
themes.evidence: The written advice notes brief references to suicide and child loss.

questions: What needs does Jesus notice in the crowd?
What can the disciples offer even when it seems small?
What do Simon and Eden struggle to communicate?
Which details appear in Matthew and which belong to the production’s imagined story?
Who might need our attention before they are ready to ask for it?

themeScripture.connection: Read the feeding of the five thousand and identify what the Gospel emphasizes before discussing how the finale presents it.

patristic.author: St. John Chrysostom
patristic.text: Chrysostom notices how readily the disciples hand over the little food they have. He draws from their response a lesson about giving to people in need even when our own resources are small.

reviews.title: Vivo
reviews.verdictRationale: Vivo keeps a commitment when it would be easier to stay with what reminds him of Andrés. His disagreements with Gabi give both characters a chance to listen to someone grieving or expressing affection in a different way. The film makes music part of honoring another person and gives kindness more weight than the brief chase and comic conflict.
reviews.ageRationale: The death of a loved one is an early emotional event. Later dangers include an encounter with a snake and some pursuit. Talk through the loss with children who have had a similar experience.
reviews.synopsis: After Andrés dies, a musical kinkajou named Vivo tries to deliver a song to the woman Andrés loved.
reviews.reflection: Ask how your family can pass on something good about a person who has died without pretending the loss is easy.

themes.name: Faithfulness and remembrance
themes.evidence: Vivo carries Andrés’s song to honor his friend’s wish.

themes.name: Friendship across differences
themes.evidence: The journey asks Vivo and Gabi to cooperate despite different temperaments.

themes.name: Grief and separation
themes.evidence: The death of Andrés drives the plot and shapes the characters’ emotions.

themes.name: Animal peril and pursuit
themes.evidence: An encounter with a snake and comic chase scenes create brief dangers.

questions: Why is the song important to Vivo?
When does Gabi help in a way he did not expect?
What helps a person remember someone who has died?
Which parts of the journey make it hard to keep a promise?
Is there a song or story we would want to share to remember somebody?

themeScripture.connection: Use Paul’s call to rejoice and weep with others to discuss which characters make room for the feelings of a friend.

reviews.title: The Croods: A New Age
reviews.verdictRationale: Grug and the Bettermans respond to unfamiliar people by trying to control family boundaries. The young people’s friendships expose what the parents miss by treating security as something they can keep to themselves. The action and jokes often exaggerate the differences, while cooperation and making room for another family carry the ending.
reviews.ageRationale: There are brief fights, sharp tools and threatening animals. The film also includes kisses and a comic allusion to nudity.
reviews.synopsis: The Croods move in with the Bettermans, and both families have to decide how much room they will make for the other.
reviews.reflection: Think of a time a rule protected a real need. Ask when the same rule might start to keep out someone who ought to be welcomed.

themes.name: Hospitality and cooperation
themes.evidence: Sharing a home and working together bring both households beyond their suspicions.

themes.name: Friendship across differences
themes.evidence: New friendships make it harder for the parents to insist on separation.

themes.name: Possessiveness and exclusion
themes.evidence: Household status and control strain relations between the families.

themes.name: Comic prehistoric peril
themes.evidence: Animal conflict and weapons add repeated bursts of danger.

questions: What makes the Bettermans feel superior at first?
Which rule makes it harder for the families to understand each other?
What do the younger characters learn before the parents do?
When do the households finally work together?
What does a visitor need besides a place to sit?

themeScripture.connection: Discuss Paul’s encouragement to practice hospitality and what accepting another household asks of both families.

reviews.title: Over the Moon
reviews.verdictRationale: Fei Fei fears a new family relationship will cost her what she had with her mother. The film takes that fear seriously and gives her reason to accept care from someone she has wanted to keep at a distance. The lunar adventure makes Chinese mythology central. The movement from clinging to the past toward accepting love gives the story the greater moral weight.
reviews.ageRationale: Bereavement and a scene centered on deep sadness may be more affecting than the fantasy scares. The story features a lunar deity, fantastical creatures and a magical potion.
reviews.synopsis: A girl who misses her mother travels to the moon hoping to prove the story of Chang’e and resist changes at home.
reviews.reflection: Ask how remembering someone and making room for a new relationship can belong in the same family.

themes.name: Openness to love after loss
themes.evidence: Fei Fei learns that welcoming people can coexist with missing her mother.

themes.name: Family patience
themes.evidence: The changes at home give Fei Fei reasons to see what others need as well.

themes.name: Grief and struggle with change
themes.evidence: Bereavement and the fear of losing family connections drive her journey.

themes.name: Mythological powers
themes.evidence: Chang’e and the magical world of the moon are central to the fantasy.

questions: Why is it hard for Fei Fei to welcome changes at home?
What does she expect the moon trip to prove?
What can she understand about Chang’e’s sadness?
How can someone joining a family honor the person who was there before?
What do we do to remember someone we miss?

themeScripture.connection: The Psalm’s attention to the brokenhearted gives families a way to start talking about Fei Fei’s grief.

reviews.title: The LEGO Movie 2: The Second Part
reviews.verdictRationale: Emmet’s impulse to trust others and Rex’s hard-edged advice point toward different ways of responding to hurt. The sibling conflict shows that assuming the worst can make creative play feel like a contest over who matters. The frequent battles are a major part of the entertainment, while the story gives the better outcome to listening and making something together.
reviews.ageRationale: Repeated explosions, fantasy weapons and separation from friends can be intense. A void sequence may scare viewers who are sensitive to losing someone.
reviews.synopsis: Emmet sets out to rescue his friends from unfamiliar newcomers while a conflict between siblings shapes the toy world.
reviews.reflection: Ask which rules can help siblings share without treating the younger one’s ideas as a problem to solve.

themes.name: Cooperation and reconciliation
themes.evidence: Making peace changes what the siblings and their characters can build together.

themes.name: Openness to another perspective
themes.evidence: The characters have to reconsider who is threatening whom.

themes.name: Fear, bitterness and betrayal
themes.evidence: Hurt and suspicion lead characters to turn on one another.

themes.name: Fantasy action and separation peril
themes.evidence: The adventure repeatedly uses toy battles and explosions for excitement.

questions: What makes the younger sibling’s ideas feel threatening?
What does Rex want Emmet to become?
Who has misunderstood somebody else?
Why is a shared world different from letting somebody borrow a toy?
What could we make together if everyone got to contribute an idea?

themeScripture.connection: Compare what it looks like to put another person’s interests into a decision with how the children share the toys.

reviews.title: Abominable
reviews.verdictRationale: Yi has withdrawn from other people in her grief. Helping Everest forces her to stay present for someone who needs a home, and it gives her friends a chance to support her. The pursuers show the cost of valuing a creature for what fame or money it might bring. The magical landscapes deepen the adventure, while loyalty and renewing family connections give it its strongest moral weight.
reviews.ageRationale: Pursuit, threats to the yeti and moments of sadness about Yi’s father call for attention. Seven is a starting point for children who can talk about animated animal peril.
reviews.synopsis: Yi and two friends try to return a young yeti to the Himalayas after finding him hiding in the city.
reviews.reflection: Ask how helping Everest home affects the way Yi thinks about her own home.

themes.name: Compassion and helping a stranger
themes.evidence: Yi takes responsibility for getting a frightened creature back to his family.

themes.name: Friendship during grief
themes.evidence: The journey gives Yi reasons to reconnect while she still misses her father.

themes.name: Exploiting a creature
themes.evidence: The pursuers treat Everest as something to capture and use.

themes.name: Fantastical powers and pursuit
themes.evidence: Everest’s powers and the danger of being caught recur through the trip.

questions: Why does Yi keep Everest’s presence secret at first?
What does the journey give her a chance to remember?
Why do other characters want to capture Everest?
When does a friend help Yi without forcing her to talk?
How could we help someone get back to a place where they feel safe?

themeScripture.connection: Read Paul on bearing burdens and consider when the friends help Yi with something she did not ask them to carry.

reviews.title: Ralph Breaks the Internet
reviews.verdictRationale: Ralph’s fear of losing his closest friend becomes a reason to interfere with her choices. The damage he causes makes the line between loyalty and control visible. The film’s jokes and chases have their own appeal, but the friendship changes for the better when Ralph accepts that staying close can require respecting a different path.
reviews.ageRationale: Threatening virus imagery, chases and suggestive online advertising are part of the setting. Ten is a starting point for talking about digital behavior and possessiveness.
reviews.synopsis: Ralph and Vanellope go online to save her game, and Ralph worries when she discovers a future he did not expect.
reviews.reflection: Ask how to be honest about missing someone while still allowing them to grow.

themes.name: Friendship and making room for change
themes.evidence: Vanellope’s new interests give both friends a choice about what their relationship can become.

themes.name: Taking responsibility and repairing harm
themes.evidence: Ralph has to confront the consequences of choices he makes in fear.

themes.name: Jealousy and control
themes.evidence: Ralph tries to keep his friend close by interfering with her plans.

themes.name: Digital fantasy peril
themes.evidence: A virus and internet-world threats drive the climactic danger.

questions: What does Vanellope find online that Ralph did not expect?
How does fear affect Ralph’s treatment of his friend?
What happens when Ralph tries to solve her decision for her?
When is giving someone space a form of loyalty?
What could you say if a friend wants to do something you do not enjoy?

themeScripture.connection: Read about love that does not insist on its own way. Compare the parts of Ralph’s conduct that fit that description with the parts that do not.

reviews.title: The Grinch
reviews.verdictRationale: The Grinch treats other people’s joy as something to take from them. Cindy Lou’s attention to someone else’s needs gives him a different experience of the holiday. The theft is playful in presentation, but its failure shows that possessions are not what holds the community together. The clearest invitation is to extend generosity even to someone who has excluded themselves.
reviews.ageRationale: The 2018 animated version has brief slapstick and minor threat. Children especially sensitive to theft or loneliness may benefit from watching with family.
reviews.synopsis: A lonely neighbor tries to stop Christmas in Whoville and discovers that taking its gifts does not end the celebration.
reviews.reflection: When the village sings, ask what the celebration still has. Read a Nativity passage if the carols prompt questions about why Christians celebrate Christmas.

themes.name: Generosity and welcome
themes.evidence: Cindy Lou’s concern for others and the town’s openness change how the Grinch sees them.

themes.name: Joy beyond possessions
themes.evidence: The celebration continues when its material things are missing.

themes.name: Resentment and theft
themes.evidence: The Grinch tries to ease his hurt by taking other people’s gifts.

themes.name: Brief comic danger
themes.evidence: Slapstick and minor threats occasionally create scares.

questions: Why does the Grinch think taking things will stop the celebration?
What is Cindy Lou concerned about besides gifts?
How does loneliness affect the way the Grinch sees the town?
What changes when people keep singing?
Who could we invite into a celebration even if they seem uninterested?

themeScripture.connection: Christ’s teaching about hospitality gives a way to discuss welcoming someone who is unlikely to return the invitation.

reviews.title: Smallfoot
reviews.verdictRationale: Migo’s encounter gives him a reason to challenge the Stonekeeper’s account. Percy is also willing to deceive people for attention, so the film puts pressure on both sides to tell the truth. That makes for a useful family conversation. The story gives a broad treatment of inherited authority and protective lies, which leaves a Christian family room to distinguish honest questions from rejecting every tradition.
reviews.ageRationale: Comic falls and brief threat accompany scenes of conflict and fear about another community. The story’s fictional creation account may invite questions from younger viewers.
reviews.synopsis: A yeti who has seen a human teams up with a television host and questions the rules keeping their communities apart.
reviews.reflection: Discuss what an adult should do when a child asks a difficult question. Consider how to keep the conversation honest if the answer is uncertain.

themes.name: Truthfulness and curiosity
themes.evidence: Migo’s experience forces the community to face a claim it would rather dismiss.

themes.name: Hospitality across fear
themes.evidence: Percy and Migo learn from meeting a person on the other side of the story.

themes.name: Deception for control or attention
themes.evidence: The Stonekeeper protects the shared account and Percy considers a false sighting for ratings.

themes.name: Animated threat
themes.evidence: The guides report brief danger and comic falls.

questions: What does Migo see that he has not been taught to expect?
Why does the Stonekeeper defend a lie?
What is Percy willing to do for his job?
Which questions help the characters understand each other?
How can we ask hard questions respectfully?

themeScripture.connection: Use Paul’s instruction to speak truthfully to discuss why the characters believe a lie might keep people safe.

reviews.title: Kubo and the Two Strings
reviews.verdictRationale: Kubo’s relatives seek to control what he sees and who he can love. The people who protect him show a different use of strength, one that allows him to remember grief without becoming indifferent to others. The film resolves the struggle through memory and compassion as well as combat. Its supernatural world and prolonged scenes of loss deserve separate discussion.
reviews.ageRationale: Sinister relatives, skeletal monsters and sword fights can be frightening. The loss of family members gives several scenes extra emotional weight.
reviews.synopsis: A young storyteller searches for protection from supernatural relatives while learning more about his parents and their sacrifices.
reviews.reflection: Ask how a family can remember pain and still choose to treat another person with mercy.

themes.name: Family love and remembrance
themes.evidence: Learning his family’s story changes what Kubo understands about their choices.

themes.name: Compassion after conflict
themes.evidence: The village responds with kindness to someone who caused harm after he loses his memory.

themes.name: Coercive control
themes.evidence: Kubo’s relatives try to decide what he can see and who he can love.

themes.name: Supernatural imagery and combat
themes.evidence: Witches, a giant skeleton and recurring sword fights make the fantasy intense.

questions: What does Kubo learn from telling his family’s story?
Why do the people who protect him accept a cost?
Which moments are about grief as much as fighting?
How does the village respond when it could hold a grudge?
What would a merciful response remember about the harm that was done?

themeScripture.connection: Christ’s call to be merciful gives a way to discuss how the village responds after the conflict.

reviews.title: Sing
reviews.verdictRationale: Buster's wish to save his theater creates a gathering place for strangers whose gifts and fears deserve attention. The story rewards practice, teamwork, courage and reconciliation, but Buster also makes exaggerated promises and the film plays questionable shortcuts for laughs. The good lessons are real without making the showbiz ambition itself a spiritual ideal; it remains mostly recreational entertainment.
reviews.ageRationale: Animated peril includes a flooded stage and pursuit by criminal bears, while animal flirting, club drinks and mild insults call for parental context. Seven and older is a cautious independent suggestion, not a rating supplied by a source.
reviews.synopsis: A koala theater owner organizes a singing contest to rescue his struggling venue, gathering performers with very different home lives.

themes.name: Courage to use a gift
themes.evidence: Several performers move from anxiety or disappointment toward a genuine attempt to sing.

themes.name: Encouragement and teamwork
themes.evidence: Performers help one another when the theater and their plans fall apart.

themes.name: Dishonest promises
themes.evidence: Buster advertises a prize he cannot pay; the crisis exposes the risk, though comic tone softens the wrongdoing.

themes.name: Animated danger and nightlife
themes.evidence: A flooding venue and club scenes create some peril and adult-setting references.

reviews.reflection: Ask whether a good dream excuses a promise we cannot keep. Consider how music can be offered generously rather than used only to win applause.
questions: Why does Buster promise more money than he can provide?
Who becomes more courageous by the time they perform?
How do different families support—or overlook—the performers?
Does talent make dishonesty acceptable if the show succeeds?
What could this group accomplish by telling the truth from the beginning?

themeScripture.connection: Discuss why honest speech matters when many people depend on one person's promises.

reviews.title: The Good Dinosaur
reviews.verdictRationale: Arlo begins as a frightened young dinosaur and gradually accepts help from someone very different from himself. The story treats grief, perseverance and returning to family as worthy of admiration; loss is not presented as a punishment for weakness. The hallucinogenic-fruit sequence is a comic exception rather than a positive model for managing fear. Its emotional center favors compassion and responsibility.
reviews.ageRationale: A parent's death, flash floods, threatening predators and a fermented-fruit hallucination make this intense for younger or bereaved viewers. Ten and older gives room to process grief and danger together.
reviews.synopsis: After a family tragedy, a young dinosaur journeys across dangerous country with a small human companion.

themes.name: Courage while afraid
themes.evidence: Arlo takes difficult steps home despite repeated fears and the memory of his father.

themes.name: Friendship across differences
themes.evidence: Arlo and Spot protect each other even when they struggle to communicate.

themes.name: Grief and intense peril
themes.evidence: The film depicts a parental death, storms and dangerous predator encounters.

themes.name: Intoxication-like joke
themes.evidence: Fermented fruit leads the companions to hallucinate; the episode is played for comedy.

reviews.reflection: The characters cannot undo their loss. Ask how a family can face fear with companionship rather than pretend the pain does not exist.
questions: What changes Arlo’s idea of what courage means?
Why does Arlo finally trust Spot?
How does losing someone change the way Arlo sees home?
Was eating the strange fruit a wise way to handle fear?
What could we do for a grieving friend rather than offering only easy answers?

themeScripture.connection: Use the call to courage as a discussion prompt, without equating the film's invented world with biblical history.

reviews.title: The Peanuts Movie
reviews.verdictRationale: Charlie Brown wants recognition but repeatedly discovers that what matters is helping others and refusing to abandon an honest effort. The story treats embarrassment and failure sympathetically rather than mocking weakness as something shameful. His final affirmation rests more on kindness and perseverance than on a perfect performance. Light teasing and imagined combat remain minor concerns.
reviews.ageRationale: Mild name-calling, childhood embarrassment and imaginary aerial fights are generally manageable for school-age children. A sensitive child may want reassurance after the teasing scenes.
reviews.synopsis: Charlie Brown attempts to impress a new classmate while facing mistakes, embarrassment and the support of his friends.

themes.name: Perseverance without applause
themes.evidence: Charlie Brown keeps trying even when his projects go badly.

themes.name: Kindness over image
themes.evidence: Concern for classmates matters more than the status he wants.

themes.name: Teasing and exclusion
themes.evidence: Children call one another names and laugh at failures, though the story ultimately favors kindness.

themes.name: Comic conflict
themes.evidence: The flying-ace scenes are playful fantasy conflict, not graphic violence.

reviews.reflection: Charlie Brown is not always rewarded at the moment he tries to do what is right. Discuss whether goodness depends on being noticed.
questions: What does Charlie Brown believe success will make other people think of him?
Which kind act does he do without expecting a reward?
When do friends help rather than mock someone’s mistake?
Can someone be a good person even after failing publicly?
Whom could we encourage this week who seems overlooked?

themeScripture.connection: Explore why continuing to do good does not always bring immediate recognition.

reviews.title: Shaun the Sheep Movie
reviews.verdictRationale: Shaun's attempt to escape ordinary farm routine causes a separation he did not intend. The animals then take responsibility and risk inconvenience to bring their farmer home. The slapstick and cheeky humor can obscure the consequences of mischief, but the emotional resolution values family loyalty and reconciliation more than rebellious fun.
reviews.ageRationale: Wordless humor includes fart jokes, brief nonsexual nudity and chasing or falling hazards. The fear of being separated from a caregiver may affect sensitive younger viewers.
reviews.synopsis: Shaun's mischievous plan sends his farmer into the city, forcing the flock to work together to bring him back.

themes.name: Loyalty and reconciliation
themes.evidence: Shaun and the flock persist until their farmer is reunited with them.

themes.name: Responsibility for mistakes
themes.evidence: The sheep try to repair the consequences of their own escape plan.

themes.name: Careless mischief
themes.evidence: The story begins by celebrating a disruptive prank before showing its costs.

themes.name: Slapstick and rude humor
themes.evidence: Cartoon falls and bodily-function jokes recur.

reviews.reflection: The plan sounded harmless before others were hurt. Ask what repentance means when someone must do more than say sorry to repair a mistake.
questions: Why did Shaun want a break from the farm routine?
When did the flock realize their joke had hurt someone?
How do they take responsibility rather than blame one another?
Who helps the animals while they are vulnerable in the city?
What would making things right look like after a similar mistake at home?

themeScripture.connection: Use the theme of returning home as an analogy for reconciliation, not a claim that the cartoon retells the parable.

reviews.title: Minions
reviews.verdictRationale: The Minions are loyal to one another, but their search for the most powerful villain makes wrongdoing appear exciting and funny. Their incompetence undercuts much of the villainy, yet there is little sustained moral reckoning with admiring criminals. This is chiefly slapstick entertainment: a family should not mistake the heroes' affection for each other as approval of their ambition to serve evil.
reviews.ageRationale: Frequent cartoon danger, weapons, villain-themed humor and a few unsettling gag sequences may overwhelm very young children. Seven and older leaves room to separate comic imitation from admirable behavior.
reviews.synopsis: A group of yellow comic sidekicks searches for a powerful villain to serve, leaving a trail of accidental chaos.

themes.name: Friendship and loyalty
themes.evidence: Kevin, Stuart and Bob support one another while their mission changes.

themes.name: Persistence
themes.evidence: They keep helping one another, but the destination of their ambition is morally misguided.

themes.name: Admiration of villainy
themes.evidence: The film treats serving villains as the characters’ cherished goal.

themes.name: Cartoon cruelty and peril
themes.evidence: Chases, weapons and slapstick torture imagery appear in comic form.

reviews.reflection: Ask whether being good at helping a friend is enough when the shared goal is wrong. Loyalty needs a worthy purpose.
questions: Why do the Minions want to find a villain?
Can someone show friendship while pursuing a harmful goal?
Does the movie reward or question the search for power?
Which funny moments should not be copied in real life?
What would a better mission for these three characters look like?

themeScripture.connection: Discuss what it means to reject evil rather than make a villain into an ideal.

reviews.title: Brother Bear
reviews.verdictRationale: Kenai's anger after family loss leads to harm, and the transformation into a bear forces him to see creatures he once blamed as members of a family. The narrative increasingly values empathy, remorse and costly reconciliation rather than revenge. Its spirit-transformation framework draws on fictionalized Indigenous spirituality; parents should discuss it as part of the story, not as a description of Orthodox teaching about the soul.
reviews.ageRationale: Two deaths, frightening animal confrontations and visible spirit imagery make this better suited to children ready to discuss grief, forgiveness and religious difference.
reviews.synopsis: A young man transformed into a bear must travel with a cub and confront the effects of his own anger.

themes.name: Compassion born from understanding
themes.evidence: Kenai comes to recognize the bear family’s grief as real and important.

themes.name: Repentance and restitution
themes.evidence: The story asks Kenai to confront how his anger hurt others.

themes.name: Revenge and animal violence
themes.evidence: A revenge-driven pursuit and animal attacks lead to bereavement.

themes.name: Spirit transformation cosmology
themes.evidence: Spirits and magical transformations are central narrative devices; this worldview is not Orthodox doctrine.

reviews.reflection: What does Kenai understand about someone else's sorrow that he could not understand while seeking revenge?
questions: Who does Kenai blame for his loss at first?
What changes when he hears Koda’s story?
How can someone show repentance after they cannot undo an injury?
How are the film’s spirit characters different from Christian teaching?
Why might mercy be harder than revenge?

themeScripture.connection: Contrast the bitterness that drives Kenai with Christian mercy and forgiveness.

reviews.title: Pocahontas
reviews.verdictRationale: The musical encourages listening across division, respecting creation and rejecting racist hostility. Those lessons deserve appreciation, but the romantic plot and neat moral resolution rewrite a difficult history, risking confusion about real injustice and the life of the historical Pocahontas. Personified nature and Grandmother Willow belong to the film's fantasy framing. Families should use the movie as a starting point for questions, not as historical education.
reviews.ageRationale: Gun violence, ethnic insults, romantic intimacy and the film’s idealized portrayal of colonization call for active discussion. Ten and older is an independent suggestion because the historical issues need explanation.
reviews.synopsis: Disney's fictionalized musical presents a romance amid conflict between English settlers and an Indigenous community.

themes.name: Peacemaking across hostility
themes.evidence: Pocahontas challenges fear and calls for human dignity amid violent conflict.

themes.name: Care for creation
themes.evidence: The film admires the natural world and resists treating land only as property to seize.

themes.name: Historical distortion
themes.evidence: A fictional romance and simplified ending can mislead viewers about real colonial history.

themes.name: Racism and armed conflict
themes.evidence: Demeaning ethnic words and gunfire appear in the conflict.

reviews.reflection: A peaceful scene in a story is not enough to tell the truth about a people’s history. Look up the real Pocahontas and the effects of colonization after viewing.
questions: What fears lead the two groups to insult one another?
How does Pocahontas try to stop violence?
Which parts of the love story should we not treat as historical facts?
Does the story show enough of the harm colonization caused?
How could we learn the actual history while respecting Indigenous people?

themeScripture.connection: Consider justice and mercy together; friendship is not a substitute for facing historical wrongs.

reviews.title: The Little Mermaid
reviews.verdictRationale: Ariel's curiosity and willingness to act offer some positive qualities, and friends work to protect her. But the story treats a secret bargain involving her voice, family and future as the route toward romantic fulfillment; it also resolves consequences through a climactic defeat of the witch. A family can enjoy the music while questioning whether a powerful attraction justifies disobedience or giving up the ability to speak for oneself.
reviews.ageRationale: Ursula’s threats and magical contracts are frightening; there is mild romantic content, peril and a transformation scene with briefly obscured nonsexual nudity. Ten and older permits a fuller conversation about the bargain.
reviews.synopsis: An adventurous mermaid signs a dangerous bargain with a sea witch to pursue life on land and a prince she admires.

themes.name: Courage and curiosity
themes.evidence: Ariel explores the human world and acts despite fear, sometimes without sound judgment.

themes.name: Friendship and rescue
themes.evidence: Her companions try to protect her when Ursula’s bargain becomes dangerous.

themes.name: Reckless romantic choice
themes.evidence: Ariel risks family ties and her voice in pursuit of a near-stranger.

themes.name: Witchcraft and coercive bargain
themes.evidence: Ursula uses an enchanted contract and transformations to manipulate victims.

reviews.reflection: Ariel gives up her voice believing she will gain something more valuable. Ask what important gifts are too easily surrendered under pressure.
questions: What attracts Ariel to the human world before she meets Eric?
Why is giving up her voice a dangerous bargain?
Which of her friends help without agreeing with every decision?
Does the happy ending erase the risk of her choice?
How could someone respond wisely to an offer that seems too good to refuse?

themeScripture.connection: Explore guarding one's judgment and affections rather than equating a fairy tale with spiritual instruction.

reviews.title: Treasure Planet
reviews.verdictRationale: Jim's frustration and recklessness make him vulnerable to someone charming but dishonest. Silver becomes a morally mixed mentor, while Jim's growth depends on trust, courage and refusing to abandon responsibility. The movie makes greed dangerous rather than the final ideal; it also leaves room to ask why a sympathetic adult can still betray someone. The adventurous setting is science fiction, not an invitation into occult practice.
reviews.ageRationale: Space battles, explosions, falls, weapons, background drinking and a smoking character make this better for older school-age viewers. Adults should discuss the complicated mentor relationship.
reviews.synopsis: A restless teenager travels with space pirates seeking treasure and finds an unlikely, unreliable mentor.

themes.name: Responsibility and courage
themes.evidence: Jim grows into a more reliable member of the expedition during dangerous moments.

themes.name: Mentorship and trust
themes.evidence: Silver teaches Jim skills but compromises the relationship through greed.

themes.name: Greed and betrayal
themes.evidence: The treasure hunt exposes how self-interest damages relationships.

themes.name: Sustained action and smoking
themes.evidence: Weapon battles and peril recur; some background characters drink or smoke.

reviews.reflection: Someone may care about us and still make selfish choices. Discuss why trust includes noticing patterns of action, not just warm words.
questions: Why does Jim feel misunderstood at the beginning?
What does Silver teach him that is genuinely useful?
When does Silver betray Jim’s trust?
Does being kind in one moment excuse betrayal in another?
What makes a mentor worthy of trust?

themeScripture.connection: Examine how companionship can support wisdom or pull someone toward greed.

reviews.title: The Jungle Book
reviews.verdictRationale: Baloo and Bagheera's protective friendship gives the story much of its heart, and Mowgli's return to other humans is treated as a question of belonging. At the same time, King Louie's portrayal and the limited agency given to some characters reflect dated stereotyping. The hypnosis scene is a cartoon threat rather than occult instruction. As a family adventure it offers good discussion, but its shortcomings prevent an uncomplicated edifying judgment.
reviews.ageRationale: Shere Khan’s threat, fire and snake hypnosis may frighten sensitive children. Parents should discuss racialized portrayals and the presentation of the human girl rather than treat them as harmless background.
reviews.synopsis: A human boy raised in the jungle is guided by animal friends as he searches for a safer place to grow up.

themes.name: Protective friendship
themes.evidence: Baloo and Bagheera risk themselves for Mowgli’s well-being.

themes.name: Courage and belonging
themes.evidence: Mowgli faces dangers while learning where he may belong.

themes.name: Racialized stereotypes
themes.evidence: The depiction of King Louie and monkeys draws on harmful dated caricature.

themes.name: Animal threat and hypnosis
themes.evidence: A tiger menace and cartoon snake hypnosis create danger without realistic injury.

reviews.reflection: A character can make us laugh while the portrayal still contains an unfair stereotype. Ask how to enjoy an old film without repeating its prejudices.
questions: How do Baloo and Bagheera show different kinds of care?
Why does Mowgli resist leaving the jungle?
What makes King Louie’s portrayal troubling today?
Why should we question a joke that depends on a stereotype?
What makes someone a true member of a family or community?

themeScripture.connection: Use the warning against favoritism to discuss judging people by a stereotype.

reviews.title: Cinderella
reviews.verdictRationale: Cinderella refuses to return cruelty for cruelty and remains considerate despite the abuse she experiences. The magical rescue is not a realistic model of how a child should escape mistreatment, nor should patience mean silently tolerating danger. The story chiefly admires kindness, friendship and hope, but families should distinguish these virtues from passivity in the face of real abuse.
reviews.ageRationale: Stepmother and stepsister cruelty, torn clothing and a chase may distress young children. Seven and older gives room to talk about asking trustworthy adults for help when mistreated.
reviews.synopsis: A mistreated young woman holds on to hope with the help of animal friends and a fairy godmother.

themes.name: Kindness in adversity
themes.evidence: Cinderella does not adopt the household’s bullying as her own way of relating to others.

themes.name: Hope and friendship
themes.evidence: Her animal friends and others assist her amid isolation.

themes.name: Family cruelty
themes.evidence: A stepmother and stepsisters mock, control and imprison Cinderella.

themes.name: Magical rescue and passivity
themes.evidence: A supernatural intervention changes Cinderella’s life while ordinary help-seeking is scarcely explored.

reviews.reflection: Cinderella is kind while she is treated unfairly. How can we value gentleness and still insist that a person in danger should seek help?
questions: What choices help Cinderella remain kind?
Which actions of the stepfamily are not just “unfriendly” but cruel?
Who helps her when she has no power in the house?
Would a child in a similar real-life situation need help from an adult?
Why can hope and speaking up for safety go together?

themeScripture.connection: Consider overcoming evil with good without suggesting that victims must endure abuse alone.

reviews.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
reviews.verdictRationale: Snow White shows generosity and the dwarfs become protective friends, but the plot also places enormous weight on beauty, envy and romantic rescue. The Queen's hatred of a young girl's appearance is plainly evil, while the story's passive heroine and magical poison are limited models for agency. The kindness is admirable; the beauty competition and the spell-driven resolution warrant family discussion.
reviews.ageRationale: The witch’s transformation, threatened murder, frightening forest and poisoned apple can unsettle younger children. Seven and older is suggested, with reassurance for children sensitive to fairy-tale terror.
reviews.synopsis: An envious queen plots against Snow White, who is sheltered by seven miners and threatened through an enchanted apple.

themes.name: Kindness and hospitality
themes.evidence: Snow White and the dwarfs develop an affectionate, caring household.

themes.name: Protection of the vulnerable
themes.evidence: The dwarfs try to keep Snow White safe from the Queen.

themes.name: Jealousy and obsession with beauty
themes.evidence: The Queen’s envy leads her to plan harm against Snow White.

themes.name: Poison and fairy-tale sorcery
themes.evidence: The Queen uses a magical mirror and enchanted poison while the forest scenes frighten Snow White.

reviews.reflection: The Queen confuses physical beauty with a person's worth. Discuss what kindness shows about a person that a mirror cannot see.
questions: Why does the Queen want to be declared the fairest?
How do the dwarfs learn to care for someone outside their family?
What makes an offer from a stranger dangerous in this story?
Does the ending ask Snow White to solve her own problems?
How would a family measure someone’s worth without discussing their looks?

themeScripture.connection: Consider the difference between outward appearance and the heart.
